A second time also the Lord threatens that he will surround Ariel with a ring, and cast up a mound against it, and set up fortifications for its siege, and that what he himself says, lamenting Jerusalem in the Gospel, will be fulfilled: If you knew the things that are for your peace, for days shall come upon you, and your enemies shall surround you with a rampart, and besiege you, and you shall be brought low to the ground (Luke 19:42ff.). And Jerusalem shall be trodden down by the nations until the time of the nations is consummated.

655. And I will encircle. Here he threatens destruction by the Romans. And concerning this, he sets out four things. First, the siege: and I will encircle you like a sphere, that is, round about: your enemies shall cast a trench about you (Luke 19:43); he shall laugh at every strong hold, and shall cast up a mount (Hab 1:10).

For in other words the prophet now says the same thing: that, brought low, it speaks from the earth, and its speech is heard from the ground; and its voice is like that of a python from the earth, and from the ground it mutters like sparrows; so that by these words he signifies the νεκυομαντείαν of the magicians, by which they are said to call up souls and to hear the thin voices of shades, or rather of demons. Indeed for python Aquila translated magician, which in Hebrew is called CHEB (כאב), for which the Seventy translated those speaking from the earth. By these words it is indicated that the ruin of the temple will remain until the consummation of the world, so that, having collapsed into ashes, it will never be raised again.

Second, the humiliation of the besieged: you shall be humbled; and the sign of their humiliation, you shall speak out of the earth, that is, just as if you were under the earth, so shall you humbly be heard, bearing the words of the python, which chanted silently: I will take away out of the midst of you your proud boasters (Zeph 3:11); or their meriting of humiliation, accusing them of the sin of avarice: you shall speak out of the earth, and idolatry: and your voice shall be like that of the python.

And so great an army of Roman power will encompass you, O Ariel, that it will be compared to countless dust, like ash flying through the air. Hence he compares to dust and ash not the weakness of those who made war against them, but their multitude, which is equal to the countless sands.

Third, he sets out the multitude of the enemy: and the multitude of them that fan you, shall be like small dust: a nation come up upon my land (Joel 1:6), or the destruction of the enemy, as above: he shall be carried away as the dust of the mountains before the wind (Isa 17:13).

And this will be suddenly, at once, so that in the midst of peace sudden wars arise under Nero, and the Lord of hosts visits Jerusalem with thunder, and with the shaking of the earth, and with the whirlwind of tempest, and with the flame of devouring fire, by which he signifies that the temple was to be burned.

Fourth, he sets out the destruction itself: and it shall be at an instant suddenly, metaphorically, because of the ferocity of the enemy: he shall come up as a cloud, and his chariots as a tempest: his horses are swifter than eagles (Jer 4:13).

And the Romans, who, when the Jews had been overcome and Jerusalem overthrown under Titus and Vespasian, offered to the Capitol spoils from the vessels that once were God's, and thought that what they had done was the work of their own valor and of the power of their gods, not of the wrath of God, will possess all their riches as in a dream and in a vision of the night. And as one who is hungry thinks, while sleeping, that he is eating in his dreams, and one who is thirsty, his throat parched with thirst, drinks rivers, and when he has awakened his thirst becomes fiercer, having been mocked by an empty drink: so the multitude of all the nations which, subject to Roman power, fought against Mount Zion, will have their riches as in a shadow and a cloud and a dream of the night, riches which they will leave behind by an early death. In the place where we have put: all who have made war and besieged and prevailed against it, the Seventy translated: and all who have fought against Jerusalem, which is not in the Hebrew.

656. And the multitude of all nations that have fought against Ariel, shall be as the dream. Here he adds some consolation from the punishment of the enemy, for like a vain thing, they will go into nothing, not carrying back anything advantageous from the destruction of Judea, just as someone hungry or thirsty gets nothing from food or drink he dreams of: the hopes of a man that is void of understanding are vain and deceitful: and dreams lift up fools (Sir 34:1); I will make Jerusalem a burdensome stone to all people (Zech 12:3).

657. Note on the words, it shall be as the dream (Isa 29:7), that something is called a dream: first, because of vanity: the vision of dreams is the resemblance of one thing to another (Sir 34:3); second, because of brevity: as a dream that flees away he shall not be found (Job 20:8); third, because of obscurity of understanding: by a dream in a vision by night (Job 33:15); fourth, because of perversity of soul, below: sleeping and loving dreams (Isa 56:10).

And those who sleep are those who, when they ought to be taking heed and watching with the soul, are not doing this. But by reason of great want of attention they are nodding in resolution and are drowsy in their reflections, such as "in their dreaming defile the flesh, and set at nothing that which is highest in authority, and rail at dignities." And these, because they are asleep, live in an atmosphere of vain and dreamlike fancies concerning realities. [They do not admit] the things that are actually true, but [they are] deceived by what appears in their vain imaginations. In regard to [them] it is said in Isaiah, "Like as when a thirsty man dreams that he is drinking, but when he has risen up is still thirsty, and his soul has cherished a vain hope, so shall be the wealth of all the nations, as many as have warred in Jerusalem."

Let us speak of him who thought he was happy since he was chief butler and believed that this was the summit and crown of all power, that he would give the cup to the king. This was his glory, this was his grandeur in this world; when he was deprived of this he felt sorrow, and when he was restored to it he rejoiced. But this is a dream, and all worldly power is a dream, not a reality. To be sure, he saw by way of a dream that his preeminent position was restored to him. Isaiah also says that people of this kind are such as take delight in prosperity in this world. One who eats and drinks in his sleep thinks he is filled with food and drink, but when he awakens, he begins to be more hungry; then he understands how insubstantial were that dreamer's food and drink. Just so, one who is asleep in this world and does not open his eyes to the mysteries of God, as long as he is in a deep corporeal sleep, supposes that such worldly power is of some importance, seeing it, as it were, in his dreams. But when he has awakened, he discovers how insubstantial the pleasure of this world is.

But that we may know that waters and cups signify teaching, the Lord speaks to the Samaritan woman: Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will not thirst for ever. Therefore whoever drinks of the waters of the Samaritan woman, that is, of the heretics, will always thirst and will not be able to cool the burning of a parched throat, as Isaiah cries aloud about this very thing: As one who is thirsty dreams that he drinks, and when he has risen he still thirsts, and his soul has hoped in vain; so shall all the nations be that fight against Jerusalem. For truly whoever drinks of the waters of the heretics, and fights against Jerusalem, the Church of God, drinks in his sleep, and his soul is mocked by empty images. And when he thinks himself satisfied, then he will have the beginning of thirst.

What are we to do now, my brothers, when crushed, cast down and drunk but not with strong drink or with wine, which excites and obfuscates but for a while, but with the blow which the Lord has inflicted upon us? He says, "And you, O heart, be stirred and shaken, and gives to the despisers the spirit of sorrow and deep sleep to drink." To [them] he also says, "See, you despisers, behold, and wonder and perish." How shall we bear his convictions; or what reply shall we make, when he reproaches us not only with the multitude of the benefits for which we have continued ungrateful, but also with his chastisements, and reckons up the remedies with which we have refused to be healed?

Since you are reasonable, I know that after my exhortation you will not permit yourselves to go beyond the bounds of what you need. But now it is appropriate for me to urge you not only to turn aside from drinking to excess but also to avoid the drunkenness that comes without drinking wine. For this kind is more dangerous. Don't be astonished at what I say, for it is possible to be drunk without wine. That you may know that this is possible, listen to the prophet, who said, "Woe to those who are drunk not from wine." But what is this drunkenness that does not come from wine? It takes many and varied forms. For anger makes us drunk; so too, vainglory, haughty madness, and all the deadly passions that spring up in us produce a kind of drunkenness and satiety that darkens our reason. For drunkenness is nothing more than the distraction of our minds from their natural ways, the straying of reason and the loss of our understanding.

Yes, it is possible to be drunk without wine; it is possible for a sober person to act as if he is drunk and to revel like a prodigal. If one could not get drunk without wine, the prophet would never have said, "Woe to those who are drunk not from wine"; if one could not get drunk without wine, Paul would never have said, "Do not be drunk with wine." For he said this as if there were a possibility of getting drunk some other way. And it is possible. A person can be drunk with anger, with unseemly desire, with greed, with vainglory, with ten thousand other passions. For drunkenness is nothing other than a loss of right reason, a derangement and depriving the soul of its health.

Be stupefied and wonder: waver and stagger, be drunk, and not with wine; reel, and not with drunkenness. For the Lord has mingled for you a spirit of deep sleep: he will close your eyes; your prophets and your princes, who see visions, he will cover. And the vision of all shall be to you like the words of a sealed book, which, when they give it to one who knows letters, they will say: Read this, and he will answer: I cannot, for it is sealed. And the book shall be given to one who does not know letters, and it shall be said to him: Read; and he will answer: I do not know letters. For spirit of deep sleep the Seventy translated compunction; Theodotion ecstasy of mind; Aquila καταφορὰν, that is, heavy sleep; which in Hebrew is called THARDEMA (תרדמה), and which Scripture records was sent by God upon Adam (Gen 2), when the woman was made from the rib of his side. And Jonah snored in this same sleep in the ship (Jonah 1). And the whole prophecy after the overthrow of Jerusalem and the temple, that is, of Ariel, is against the scribes and Pharisees, who, having the key of knowledge, neither enter themselves nor allow others who wish to enter. And they are commanded to be made drunk with stupor and wonder, or rather, according to the Septuagint, with the dissolution of the whole body and ecstasy of mind, and to reel and waver: staggering not with wine nor strong drink, but with the spirit of deep sleep, or of the Lord's compunction, so that, understanding their evil, they may at some time do penance and say with the prophet: I was turned in my weakness, while the thorn is fastened in me (Ps 31 [32]:4). Know, then, O scribes and Pharisees, who are the princes of the Jews, that the Lord is repaying you in kind. For when you heard the Lord the Savior, you would not understand, and you closed your eyes lest you should see him, and made your ears heavy lest you should hear. Therefore he too will close your eyes, which are the prophets, through whom you used to see the knowledge of God. Or he will close your eyes and those of the prophets, who are your princes. For the Law and the prophets were until John the Baptist (Luke 16): so that while you do not see, those may see of whom the later passage (cf. v. 18) testifies: And in that day the deaf shall hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind shall see and exult. For the Lord came for judgment, that the Jews who see might not see, and that those who were blind, namely the people of the nations, might see and contemplate the Lord (John 9).

But we should notice the ways in which the Lord points out that the soul is weighed down: for He did not mention adultery, or fornication, or murder, or blasphemy, or rapine, which everybody knows to be deadly and damnable, but surfeiting and drunkenness, and the cares or anxieties of this world: which men of this world are so far from avoiding or considering damnable that actually some who (I am ashamed to say) call themselves monks entangle themselves in these very occupations as if they were harmless or useful. And though these three things, when literally given way to weigh down the soul, and separate it from God, and bear it down to things earthly, yet it is very easy to avoid them, especially for us who are separated by so great a distance from all converse with this world, and who do not on any occasion have anything to do with those visible cares and drunkenness and surfeiting. But there is another surfeiting which is no less dangerous, and a spiritual drunkenness which it is harder to avoid, and a care and anxiety of this world, which often ensnares us even after the perfect renunciation of all our goods, and abstinence from wine and all feastings and even when we are living in solitude-and of such the prophet says: "Awake, ye that are drunk but not with wine;" and another: "Be astonished and wonder and stagger: be drunk and not with wine: be moved, but not with drunkenness." And of this drunkenness the wine must consequently be what the prophet calls "the fury of dragons": and from what root the wine comes you may hear: "From the vineyard of Sodom," he says, "is their vine, and their branches from Gomorrha." Would you also know about the fruit of that vine and the seed of that branch? "Their grape is a grape of gall, theirs is a cluster of bitterness" for unless we are altogether cleansed from all faults and abstaining from the surfeit of all passions, our heart will without drunkenness from wine and excess of any feasting be weighed down by a drunkenness and surfeiting that is still more dangerous.
The First Conference of Abbot Isaac, Chapter 5

658. Be astonished. Here he threatens the punishment of blinding, and first, he foretells the blinding of the Jews; second, the conversion of the gentiles: is it not yet a very little while (Isa 29:17). Concerning the first, he does two things: first, he sets out the blinding; second, he assigns the reason for it: and the Lord said (Isa 29:13).

659. Concerning the first, he does three things. First, he foretells the blinding, setting out those things which confused the judgment of their reason: be astonished, from consideration of the guilt of the wicked or of their punishment: be astonished, O you heavens, at this, and you gates thereof, be very desolate (Jer 2:12); and wonder, from consideration of great things: wonderful are your works (Ps 138[139]:14); waver, from uncertainty in choosing: for he that wavers is like a wave of the sea, which is moved and carried about by the wind (Jas 1:6); stagger, from inconstancy of intention: your hands have confirmed them that were staggering (Job 4:4); be drunk, from anxiety of sorrows: drink you also, and fall fast asleep: the cup of the right hand of the Lord shall compass you (Hab 2:16).

Not to recognize sins lest penance follow is the wrath of God, as it is written: "And the Lord gave to them the spirit of a deep sleep," lest they actually return and be cured and be healed by their lamentations and just satisfactions after their sins.…The first degree of felicity is not to sin; the second, to recognize the sins committed. In the former, innocence runs upright and unimpaired to save; in the latter, there follows the remedy to cure. They have lost both of these by offending God.… Or do you think, brother, that crimes against God are light matters, small and of little moment, because through them the majesty of an offended God is not sought, because the wrath and fire and day of the Lord are not feared, because, with Antichrist at hand, the faith of a militant people is disarmed while vigor and the fear of Christ are taken away?

Second, he sets out the manner of blinding: for the Lord has mingled for you the spirit of a deep sleep, that is, as if he offered mixed wine to drink; he will shut up your eyes, namely, the prophets, above: the Lord has mingled in the midst thereof the spirit of giddiness (Isa 19:14).

And that the things spoken of old by the law and the prophets were all sealed, and that they were unknown to people, Isaiah declares when he says, "And they will deliver the book that is sealed to one that is learned, and will say to him, 'Read this;' and he will say, 'I cannot read it, for it is sealed.' " It was right and necessary that the things spoken of old by the prophets should be sealed to the unbelieving Pharisees, who thought that they understood the letter of the law, and be opened to the believing. The things, therefore, which of old were sealed, are now by the grace of God the Lord all open to the saints.

And plainly, if we hear negligently, if we bring no zeal to erudition and understanding, not only the Scripture of the law and the prophets, but even that of the Apostles and the Gospels is covered from us with a great veil. But I fear lest, through excessive negligence and dullness of heart, the divine volumes be for us not only veiled but even sealed, so that, "if a book to be read is given into the hands of a man who does not know letters, he says: I do not know letters; if it is given into the hands of a man who knows letters, he says: it is sealed." Whence it is shown that we must not only apply zeal to learning the sacred letters, but must also entreat the Lord and "day and night" beseech him, that the Lamb "from the tribe of Judah" may come and himself, taking the "sealed book," may deign to open it. For he it is who, "opening the Scriptures," kindled the hearts of the disciples, so that they said: "was not our heart burning within us, when he opened to us the Scriptures?"

Isaiah [prophesied] that the Jews would not understand the holy Scriptures, but that they would become intelligible in the last times, after Christ had come: "And all these words shall be to you as the words of a book that is sealed, which, if you shall give to a man that knows letters to read, he shall say, I cannot read, for it is sealed.… But in that day the deaf shall hear the words of the book, and they who are in darkness and in a cloud; the eyes of the blind shall see."
Treatise XII. Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews 1:4

Instead of "Seal the vision and the prophet,'' Aquila gives, I think, a more suitable rendering, viz. "And for fulfilling vision and prophet." For our Lord Jesus Christ did not come as it were to seal up the visions of the prophets, for He rather opened and explained those that were of old obscure and sealed, tearing away so to say the seals impressed on them, and taught His disciples the meaning of the Holy Scriptures. Hence He says, "Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah hath prevailed, and he has opened the seals that were set on the book," in John's Apocalypse. What are these seals but the obscurities of the prophets? Isaiah knew them well and definitely says too: "And these words shall be as the words of the sealed book." The Christ of God did not come then to shut up the vision and the prophet, but rather to open them and bring them to the light.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 8, Chapter 2

[Daniel 12:4] "But Thou, O Daniel, shut up the words and seal the book, even to the time appointed. Many shall pass over, and knowledge shall be manifold." He who had revealed manifold truth to Daniel now signifies that the things he has said are matters of secrecy, and he orders him to roll up the scroll containing his words and set a seal upon the book, with the result that many shall read it and inquire as to its fulfilment in history, differing in their opinions because of its great obscurity. And as for the statement, "Many shall pass over" or "go through," this indicates that it will be read by many people. For it is a familiar expression to say: "I have gone through a book," or, "I have passed through an historical account." Indeed this is the idea which Isaiah also expressed in regard to the obscurity of his own book: "And the sayings of that book shall be like the words of a book that is sealed. And if they shall give it to an illiterate man, saying, 'Read it,' he will reply, 'I do not know how to read.' But if they give it to a man who does know how to read and say, 'Read the book,' he will reply, 'I cannot read it, because it is sealed up'" (Isaiah 29:11-12). Also in the Revelation of John, there is a book seen which is sealed with seven seals inside and outside. And when no one proves able to break its seals, John says, "I wept sore; and a voice came to me, saying, 'Weep not: behold the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has prevailed to open the book and break its seals'" (Revelation 5:1-5). But that book can be opened by one who has learned the mysteries of Scripture and understands its hidden truths, and its words which seem dark because of the greatness of the secrets they contain. He it is who can interpret the parables and transmute the letter which killeth into the spirit which quickeneth.
St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER TWELVE

Since, therefore, the teachers of the Jews to this present day cannot read and open the seals and lay open the mysteries of the Scriptures, if you give that book to the unlearned people, who are devoured by their own teachers, they will confess that they do not know letters and therefore cannot read. And of two evils it is much lighter to confess ignorance of the Law than to boast of wisdom and not be able to know what is said.

But Thou, O Daniel, shut up the words and seal the book, even to the time appointed. Many shall pass over, and knowledge shall be manifold. He who had revealed manifold truth to Daniel now signifies that the things he has said are matters of secrecy, and he orders him to roll up the scroll containing his words and set a seal upon the book, with the result that many shall read it and inquire as to its fulfilment in history, differing in their opinions because of its great obscurity. And as for the statement, "Many shall pass over" or "go through," this indicates that it will be read by many people. For it is a familiar expression to say: "I have gone through a book," or, "I have passed through an historical account." Indeed this is the idea which Isaiah also expressed in regard to the obscurity of his own book: "And the sayings of that book shall be like the words of a book that is sealed. And if they shall give it to an illiterate man, saying, 'Read it,' he will reply, 'I do not know how to read.' But if they give it to a man who does know how to read and say, 'Read the book,' he will reply, 'I cannot read it, because it is sealed up.'" Also in the Revelation of John, there is a book seen which is sealed with seven seals inside and outside. And when no one proves able to break its seals, John says, "I wept sore; and a voice came to me, saying, 'Weep not: behold the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has prevailed to open the book and break its seals.'" But that book can be opened by one who has learned the mysteries of Scripture and understands its hidden truths, and its words which seem dark because of the greatness of the secrets they contain. He it is who can interpret the parables and transmute the letter which killeth into the spirit which quickeneth.

In the Apocalypse a book is shown sealed with seven seals, which if you deliver to one that is learned saying, "Read this," he will answer you, "I cannot, for it is sealed." How many there are today who fancy themselves learned, yet the Scriptures are a sealed book to them, and one which they cannot open save through him who has the key of David, "he that opens and no man shuts; and shuts and no man opens." In the Acts of the Apostles the holy eunuch when reading Isaiah is asked by Philip, "Do you understand what you are reading?" The man answered, "How can I, except some man should guide me?" To digress for a moment to myself, I am neither holier nor more diligent than this eunuch, who came from Ethiopia … and was so great a lover of the law and of divine knowledge that he read the holy Scriptures even in his chariot. Yet although he had the book in his hand and took into his mind the words of the Lord, no, even had them on his tongue and uttered them with his lips, he still did not know him, who—not knowing—he worshiped in the book. Then Philip came and showed him Jesus, who was concealed beneath the letter. Wondrous excellence of the teacher! In the same hour the eunuch believed and was baptized; he became one of the faithful and a saint. He was no longer a pupil but a master; and he found more in the church's font there in the wilderness than he had ever done in the gilded temple of the synagogue. These instances have been just touched upon by me (the limits of a letter forbid a more discursive treatment of them) to convince you that in the Holy Scriptures you can make no progress unless you have a guide to show you the way.

Hence he significantly did not say that the vision of all the prophets is sealed to all who read; but to you, he says, it shall be sealed, to whom I now speak, to whom I foretell that these things will come; or he will close forever the eyes of your princes, who, according to the Septuagint, boasted that they saw things hidden and secret. And all holy Scripture, he says, shall be to you closed and sealed, so that you, who suppose you know the letters of the Law and the oracles of the prophets, and meditate day and night with unwearied mouth on the volumes of the Scriptures, may not understand what you read; as it is written in the Apocalypse of John: Who is worthy to open the book and to loose its seals (Rev 5:2)? And when no one had been found to open the seals, he says that he wept, and that at last he was granted a word of God to him: Do not weep: behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has prevailed to open the book and to loose its seals. The lion of the tribe of Judah is the Lord Jesus Christ, who loosed the seals of the book, not, properly, of one book, as many think, the psalms of David, but of all the Scriptures, which were written by one Holy Spirit; and therefore they are called one book. Of this Ezekiel testifies in mystical speech (Ezek 2) that it was written within and without: in the sense and in the letter. Of this the Savior too speaks in the psalms: At the head of the book it is written of me (Ps 39 [40]:8); not of Jeremiah, not of Isaiah, but in all holy Scripture, which is called one book.

This is also why Isaiah would say to the Jews: "Behold, all of these words will be to you like the words of a sealed book." The skilled reader and the illiterate are equally said to be deprived of fruit, since one is prevented by the seal from penetrating what lies hidden within and the other is shackled by ignorance.

Sacred Scripture is compared to the water of the sea on account of the profundity of its mysteries. Hence Isaiah says: "The vision of all things shall be to you as the words of a sealed book, which when they give to one who knows letters, they will say: Read this; and he will answer: I cannot, for it is sealed. It is necessary, therefore, that one have both learning and the spirit.

What is this obstinacy or what is this presumption to place human tradition before the divine plan and not to notice that God is offended and angered as often as human tradition subverts and disregards the divine precepts? He cries and says through Isaiah, the prophet, "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far separated from me. For the speaking in this way or in that is not the cause of the thought within us; but the hidden conception of the heart supplies the motive for such and such words; "for from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh." We make the words interpret the thought; we do not by a reverse process gather the thought from the words. Should both be at hand, a man may certainly be ready in both, in clever thinking and clever expression; but if the one should be wanting, the loss to the illiterate is slight, if the knowledge in his soul is perfect in the direction of moral goodness. "This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." What is the meaning of that? That the right attitude of the soul towards the truth is more precious than the propriety of phrases in the sight of God, who hears the "groanings that cannot be uttered." Phrases can be used in opposite senses; the tongue readily serving, at his will, the intention of the speaker; but the disposition of the soul, as it is, so is it seen by Him Who sees all secrets.

Again the form of righteousness is described and magnified when Scripture says, "The law of his God is in his heart, and his stride will not be broken." The law of God is in the heart of the righteous. Which law? It is not the written law but the natural law, because "the law was not laid down for the righteous but for the unrighteous." The law is in his heart, not superficially, as it is on the lips of the Jews, for "he who believes with his heart is justified." The one who believes also speaks, but the one who speaks does not necessarily believe. For instance, the people did not believe about whom it is written: "This people honors me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me."

You understand what I said. I called those neighbours who “drew nigh,” and at the same time “stood afar off.” For they “drew nigh” in the body, but “stood afar off” in their heart. Who were in the body so near to Him as those who lifted Him on the Cross? Who in heart so far off as those who blasphemed Him? Hear this sort of distance described by the Prophet Isaiah; observe this nearness and distance at one and the same time. “This people honours Me with their lips:” behold, with their body they draw near; “but their heart is far from Me.” The same persons are at the same time “near” and “afar off” also: with their lips they are near, in heart afar off.

For God is necessary to all things, but nothing is necessary to him. He gave not only the bread of angels, therefore, but also the flesh of innumerable birds to the concupiscent, even to the ungrateful. They think God does not know their counsels because their works are in darkness, and they say: Who sees us? and who knows us? And the wise of this world, and the teachers of the heretics, and the Pharisees of the Jews say this: that no one understands them; not remembering what is said to God: Darkness shall not be dark to you: and the night shall be lit up as the day (Ps 138 [139]:12). And: As is his darkness, so also is his light (Gen 3). Deceived by this error, Adam and Eve, hearing the sound of the feet of God walking in paradise, hid themselves under the tree in which was the knowledge of good and evil; and Cain too, saying: If you cast me out today from your face, I shall be hidden (Gen 4:14), with like folly thought that God did not know. And through Amos it is said of the ungodly and sinners: If they hide themselves from my eyes in the depth of the sea, there I will command the serpent, and it shall bite them (Amos 9:3). Hence, however wise someone may be and of the most ardent talent, if he does not have the wisdom and teaching of God, let us say of him: Unless the Lord builds the house, they labor in vain who build it. Unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it watches in vain (Ps 126 [127]:1). And let us make a saying like it: Unless the Lord helps knowledge, he labors in vain who thinks himself wise. Unless the Lord keeps our heart with all watchfulness, he watches in vain who thinks it can be kept by his own diligence.

661. Woe to you that are deep of heart. Here he sets out their sin on the part of the intellect, for they did not believe in the providence of God, that he knew what happens among us. And concerning this, he does two things. First, the devising of error is set out, and they said this was hidden from God because of the depth of their heart, where they handled their wicked counsels; hence he says: woe to you that are deep of heart: the heart is deep above all things, and unsearchable, who can know it? (Jer 17:9); and because of the darkness of the places in which they carried out wicked deeds; hence he says: their works are in the dark: every one that doth evil hates the light (John 3:20); say not: I shall be hidden from God (Sir 16:16).

And not only this; but when Rebecca also had conceived by one, even by our father Isaac;  (For the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth;)  It was said unto her, The elder shall serve the younger.  As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated.  What shall we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? God forbid.  For he saith to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion.  So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that showeth mercy.  For the scripture saith unto Pharaoh, Even for this same purpose have I raised thee up, that I might show my power in thee, and that my name might be declared throughout all the earth.  Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth.  Thou wilt say then unto me, Why doth he yet find fault? For who hath resisted his will?  Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus? [Isaiah 29:16] Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?  What if God, willing to show his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction:  And that he might make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy, which he had afore prepared unto glory,  Even us, whom he hath called, not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles?

If a man seems more comely to look upon than clay, this difference was not produced by a change of nature but by the wisdom of the craftsman. Why? Because you are no different from the clay. If you refuse to believe this, let the coffins and the cinerary urn convince you. And you will know that this is the truth if you have gone to visit the tombs of your forebearers. Therefore there is no difference between the clay and the potter.

This thought of yours, he says, is perverse: that you should think the maker does not know what he has made, and the Creator is ignorant of his creature; as if the clay and the work should say to the potter and its maker: You did not make me, or you did not make me well, nor do you understand your handiwork. The Apostle uses this testimony in other words in writing to the Romans, where he discusses the deep knowledge of God and seeks to refute the false charge of men: O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to him who formed it: Why have you made me thus? Or has not the potter power over the same clay to make one vessel unto honor and another unto dishonor (Rom 9:20-21). In all these that rule must always be observed: the Evangelists and Apostles translated from the Hebrew into Greek as seemed good to them, without loss to the sense.

Scripture says to Pharaoh, "To this purpose have I raised you that I may show my power in you; and that my name may be declared throughout all the earth." Then, making a conclusion to both passages, he says, "Therefore he has mercy on whom he will and whom he will he hardens." Obviously he treats neither of these with injustice but both with mercy and truth; in spite of that there is an uprising of insolent weakness on the part of those who attempt to comprehend the unsearchable depth of the judgment of God according to the interpretations of the human heart. The apostle refutes this view when he says, "You will say therefore to me: Why does he then find fault? For who resists his will?" Let us imagine this as said to us. What other answer should we make than the one he made? If such ideas disturb us also because we, too, are human, we all have need to listen to the apostle saying, "O man, who are you that replies against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it: Why have you made me thus? Or has not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honor, another unto dishonor?" If this lump of clay were of such indifferent value that it deserved nothing good any more than it deserved anything evil, there would be reason to see injustice in making of it a vessel unto dishonor. But when, through the free will of the first man alone, condemnation extended to the whole lump of clay, undoubtedly if vessels are made of it unto honor, it is not a question of justice not forestalling grace, but of God's mercy. If, however, vessels are made of it unto dishonor, it is to be attributed to the judgment of God, not to his injustice—far be from us the thought that there could be any such with God! Whoever is wise in this matter with the Catholic church does not argue against grace in favor of merit, but he sings mercy and judgment to the Lord, that he may not ungratefully deny his mercy or unjustly upbraid his judgment.

God comes down to the level of sinful men and women; the good Lord speaks with his rebellious servants; the holy one calls those who are impure to forgiveness. Humanity created out of mud addresses its Fashioner with familiarity; dust converses with its Maker. Let us, therefore, show awe when we sinners stand in the presence of this Majesty and speak. Even though we are so impure in our deeds, he draws us close to the sight of himself in the spirit; let us therefore repeat with trembling the words of the blessed prophet Isaiah: "Woe is me, for I am dazed: I am a man of unclean lips, yet my eyes have beheld the King, the Lord Almighty."

662. Second, the just rebuke is set out, this thought of yours is perverse. You made me not, for God knows a thing in as much as he is its cause, below: woe to him that gainsays his maker (Isa 45:9), below: and now, O Lord, you are our father, and we are clay: and you are our maker, and we all are the works of your hands (Isa 64:8).

Is it not yet a little while, and a short time, and Lebanon shall be turned into Charmel, and Charmel shall be reckoned as a forest? And in that day the deaf shall hear the words of the book, and out of darkness and gloom the eyes of the blind shall see. And the meek shall increase their joy in the Lord, and the poor among men shall exult in the Holy One of Israel: for he who prevailed has failed. The scorner is consumed, and all who watched for iniquity have been cut down: who made men sin by a word, and tripped up him who reproved in the gate, and turned aside in vain from the righteous. Let the Jews answer, and the friends of the bare history alone, who seek not fruit on the tree but only the leaves and the shade of words, which quickly withers and perishes: how at the coming of the Lord the Savior (since from the times of Isaiah to the dispensation of the flesh he assumed is, compared with eternity, a short and little space of time) Lebanon, a mountain of Phoenicia, was turned and transferred into Mount Carmel, which in Hebrew is called CHERMEL (כרמל), and lies on the border of Palestine and Phoenicia, overlooking Ptolemais (though another mountain too is called Carmel in the holy Scriptures, where lived Nabal the Carmelite (1 Sam 25), a foolish and wicked man, who had as wife Abigail, who on her husband's death married David; for while he lived she could not take David as husband, lest she be called an adulteress if she were joined to another man); and how Charmel is reckoned as a forest and as unfruitful trees? Since they cannot say this, let them hear that Lebanon, which means whitening, refers to the people of the nations, which, washed in the Lord and its former filth purged away, ascending wholly clean, leans upon the Savior in the person of the Church; and of it it is said in the Song of Songs: Who is this who comes up whitened, leaning upon her kinsman (Song 8:5); and that this people is transferred into Charmel, that is, into the knowledge of circumcision, so as to recognize the mysteries of the spiritual and true circumcision, and to be in the place once held by the people of the Jews; while those who would not receive Christ are reckoned as a forest and as barren trees, which cannot praise the Lord with the fruit-bearing trees.

Note that [Paul] taught Greeks in Jerusalem, and Jews in Damascus which is a Gentile city, even though this should signify that Gentiles were to be included in the city of God and Jews were to fall into the faithlessness of the Gentiles, in accordance with what Isaiah said, "Lebanon shall be changed into Carmel, and Carmel shall be regarded as a wasteland."

663. Is it not yet a very little while? Here he foretells the conversion of the gentiles, and concerning this, he does three things. First, he foretells their conversion to grace: Libanus, a gentile people, for the mountain was in the land of the gentiles; into Carmel, into grace, which the Jews had through circumcision, because Carmel means "knowledge of circumcision"; as a forest, that is, as barrenness, which the gentiles were in before, below (Isa 32:15) has the same thing.

666. Or this may be otherwise explained as concerning the prosperity that was promised to them when Sennacherib or Nabuchodonosor were destroyed: Carmel shall be esteemed as a forest (Isa 29:17), that is, the fertility of the land of the promise will be such that the fertility of Carmel will be reckoned barrenness in comparison to it.

When Lebanon has been changed into Charmel, and Charmel into a forest, then those who before were deaf and could not hear the words of the prophetic book (of which we said above that all holy Scripture is called one book, as the Preacher says (Eccl 12:11): The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fixed deep, which are given from the councils by one shepherd) shall hear, and shall speak, those to whom the Savior will say: Ephphetha, which means be opened (Mark 7). And where we translated: out of darkness and gloom the eyes of the blind shall see, whose interpretation is easy, Aquila and Theodotion and Symmachus translated: The eyes of the blind shall see darkness and gloom: to show that the mysteries of Christ were to be laid open to the people of the nations, which before was blind, according to what is said: Dark water in the clouds of the air (Ps 17 [18]:12). And in the same psalm it is written of God: He made darkness his hiding place (ibid., 12). And in Proverbs we read: A wise man hearing these things will be wiser, and the prudent will possess government; and he will understand a parable and dark speech, the sayings of the wise and riddles (Prov 1:5-6). Indeed Moses too, that he might understand and see God (Exod 20), entered into the cloud and into the thick darkness, of which it is said in the Psalm: Thick darkness under his feet (Ps 17 [18]:10).

Neither was heaven created in any six-day period and the stars illuminated and the dry land separated from the water and the trees and vegetation planted. Rather, Scripture customarily uses "day" to denote an unspecified period of time, as the apostle did when he said, "Behold, this is the day of salvation." He was not referring to a particular day but to the entirety of the time of the present life in which we labor for eternal salvation. The prophet also spoke not of one specific day but of numerous moments of divine grace, saying, "In that day, the deaf will hear the words of this book." Moreover, it is difficult to understand how in one day God made heaven and earth and all the brush of the field and every plant of every region, unless we say that all creatures were created simultaneously in formless matter, according to which it is written: "He who lives forever created all things together."

To sacred knowledge: the deaf, namely, the gentiles, who had not heard the words of the law before: the blind see (Matt 11:5); for judgment I am come into this world: that they who see not may see; and they who see may become blind (John 9:39).

When those who were before blind have either beheld all the mystical things, or have lifted their eyes from blindness and darkness to see, so that the true light may rise for those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death: then the meek, of whom it is written: Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth (Matt 5:4); or the poor, whose prince says in the psalms: This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him (Ps 33 [34]:7); and: who shall judge the poor of the people, and shall save the sons of the poor (Ps 71 [72]:4), of whom it is said to the Jews: You have despised the counsel of the poor man: these shall increase their joy in the Lord, so that he who glories may glory in the Lord (2 Cor 10); and the poor among men, or those despaired of and despised by men, who before had no knowledge of the Law, shall exult in the Holy One of Israel, who says: Be holy, for I am holy (Lev 11:44).
To spiritual joy: and the meek shall increase their joy: I will be glad, and rejoice in you: I will sing to your name, O you Most High (Ps 9:3[2]).

And there is every exultation, because he who prevailed has failed. The scorner is consumed, or the arrogant and proud one, who had said: By strength I will do it, and by wisdom; I will remove the bounds of the nations and lay waste their strength; who mocked all, so much so that the saint too said: My loins are filled with illusions (Ps 37 [38]:8). And all who watched for iniquity have been cut down, or destroyed, whose destruction, because of their evil watchings, does not slumber: who made the whole race of men sin by a word of blasphemy, so that they denied the Word of God and set their mouth against heaven. He means the demons, who, wicked themselves, made all men sin in speech, blaspheming with various dogmas; and as far as in them lay they tripped up him who reproved in the gate and in judgment, and made him turn aside from righteousness, who was in the gates of the daughter of Zion, lifted up from the gates of death; and who rebuked those who hated him who reproved in the gates. What we have understood of the devil and his angels, the Nazarenes think was said against the scribes and Pharisees: that the δευτερωταί have failed, who before mocked the people with most wicked traditions, and watched day and night to deceive the simple, who made men sin against the Word of God, so that they denied Christ the Son of God.

664. Second, he indicates the occasion or the reason of their conversion: from the fall of the devil: for he that did prevail, by power, has failed, the scorner, the deceiver by cunning, above: the wretch is consumed: he has failed, that trod the earth under foot (Isa 16:4); from the blindness of the Jewish people, that blindness in part has happened in Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in (Rom 11:25). They are cut off that watched: zeal to do evil: for they sleep not, except they have done evil (Prov 4:16).

666. Or this may be otherwise explained as concerning the prosperity that was promised to them when Sennacherib or Nabuchodonosor were destroyed: the scorner (Isa 29:20), Sennacherib or Nabuchodonosor.

That made men sin, by wicked example and teaching; that reproved them in the gate, as to contempt of instruction: they have hated him that rebukes in the gate (Amos 5:10); and declined in vain from the just, as to the vanity of sin, for that is vain, which fails to attain its end: what has pride profited us? Or what advantage has the boasting of riches brought us? (Wis 5:8).

Therefore thus says the Lord to the house of Jacob, he who redeemed Abraham: Jacob shall not now be confounded, nor shall his face now blush: but when he sees his sons, the works of my hands, in his midst sanctifying my name: and they shall sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and shall proclaim the God of Israel; and those who err in spirit shall know understanding, and the mutterers shall learn the Law. LXX: Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the house of Jacob, which he separated from Abraham: Jacob shall not now be confounded, nor shall he now change his face; but when he sees his sons, my works: for my sake they shall sanctify my name, and they shall sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and shall fear the God of Israel; and those who err in spirit shall know understanding, and the mutterers shall learn obedience; and what follows, ÷ and the stammering tongues shall learn to speak peace ⁚, is to be marked with an obelus. When, he says, the deaf have heard the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind have seen, and Lebanon has been turned into Charmel, and Charmel reckoned as a forest, so that the meek and the poor rejoice in the Lord, and the proud man and the scorner fail: then Jacob shall be confounded, who now, for the time being, is not confounded. He means the times of Isaiah. And his face shall blush, so that blushing and confusion may be an occasion of salvation, especially when he sees his sons, that is, the Apostles and apostolic men, who were of the race of the Jews, performing the mighty works of the Lord in the midst of the nations, and proclaiming the name of Christ to the Gentiles, and saying: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name (Matt 6:9). For they will sanctify the Holy One who sprang from Jacob, and will teach the God of Israel among the nations, so that, having abandoned idols, they say: How false are the idols our fathers possessed, and there is none among them who gives rain; and then those who now err in spirit shall know the understanding of God, and those who once murmured against the Lord in the wilderness shall learn the Law, of which before they had no knowledge. For if they had received Moses, they would have received the Lord Jesus Christ too, since Moses spoke of him.

What at the beginning of the chapter we translated according to the Hebrew: Thus says the Lord to the house of Jacob, he who redeemed once Abraham, and brought him out of the Chaldeans, and led him into the land of promise (Gen 11), is perfectly plain. But what the Seventy translated: Thus says the Lord concerning the house of Jacob, which he separated from Abraham, can be understood thus: that he separated the scribes and Pharisees, who blasphemed the Lord, from Abraham, who saw the day of the Lord and rejoiced (John 8). For if they had been sons of Abraham, they would have done the works of Abraham. And the Apostle argues that those are to be called sons of Abraham (Heb 11) who have the likeness of Abraham's faith, that is, the people of the nations, which was called the son of Abraham not from works but from faith.

665. Third, he sets out the conversion of the Jews at the end of the world, when he says: therefore thus says the Lord that redeemed Abraham, Genesis 11; Jacob shall not now, that is, at this time, be confounded, by a good confounding: there is a confounding that brings glory and grace (Sir 4:25).

His children, the Apostles.

666. Or this may be otherwise explained as concerning the prosperity that was promised to them when Sennacherib or Nabuchodonosor were destroyed: he shall see his children . . . sanctifying my name (Isa 29:23), the three children in the furnace of fire; or that their children will praise my name, because they themselves in their youth did not.
They that murmured, that is, who at first murmured, above: when they shall rush out from Jacob, Israel shall blossom (Isa 27:6).
30: Reprimand is disapproval expressed in correction or strongly worded blame. The Educator resorts to this method of training when he says through Isaiah, "Woe to you, apostate children, says the Lord, that you would take counsel and not of me, and make treaties and not of my Spirit." He flavors each pronouncement in turn with the tart spice of fear to whet the appetite of his people for salvation and make them more aware of it, just as wool to be dyed is usually steeped first in an astringent to prepare it to preserve the dye.

Moreover, in the same [Gospel] he also says, "All who have come before are thieves and robbers." Who are such but the deserters of the faith and the transgressors of God's church, who strive against God's ordinance—whom the Holy Spirit rightly rebukes by the prophet, saying, "You have taken counsel, but not by me; and have made a confederacy, but not by my Spirit, to add sin to sin."

Let every man and woman among us, whether meeting together at church, or remaining at home, call upon God with much earnestness, and He will doubtless accede to these petitions. Whence does this appear evident? Because He is exceedingly desirous, that we should always take refuge in Him, and in everything make our requests unto Him; and do nothing and speak nothing without Him. For men, when we trouble them repeatedly concerning our affairs, become slothful and evasive, and conduct themselves unpleasantly towards us; but with God it is quite the reverse. Not when we apply to him continually respecting our affairs, but when we fail to do so, then is he especially displeased. Hear at least what He reproves the Jews for, when He says, "Ye have taken counsel, but not of Me, and made treaties, but not by My Spirit." For this is the custom of those who love; they desire that all the concerns of their beloved should be accomplished by means of themselves; and that they should neither do anything, nor say anything, without them. On this account did God not only on that occasion, but again elsewhere, uttering a reproof, speak the same language. "They have reigned, but not by Me; they have ruled, and they made it not known to Me." Let us not then be slow to take refuge in Him continually; and whatever be the evil, it will in any case find its appropriate solution.

Some think this place was written against the ten tribes in Samaria, because, seeking help from the Egyptians, they were taken captive by the Assyrians. According to tropology: all who, despising the religion of God, return to their vomit, and, having lost the name of sons, are called most shameless dogs, take counsel not through the Lord, and strike a covenant not through the spirit of the Lord, and add sins to sins: so that, overcome by flattering vices, they also accept the perversity of false doctrines, and go down into the darkness of Egypt, seeking the help of Pharaoh, who reigns in Egypt, whose protection leads to disgrace and to everlasting reproach. For his princes are in Tanis, that is, in a humble and lowly command, most evil messengers, who labor in vain over a people that will not be able to profit them. For as the salvation of their disciples helps holy teachers, so the perdition of those seduced destroys the patriarchs of those who have fled to the help of Egypt.

Woe, you deserting sons, says the Lord: that you should take counsel, and not from me; and weave a web, and not by my Spirit; that you might add sin upon sin. You who walk to go down into Egypt, and have not asked my mouth, hoping for help in the strength of Pharaoh, and having confidence in the shadow of Egypt. And the strength of Pharaoh shall be to you for confusion, and the confidence in the shadow of Egypt for disgrace. For your princes shall be in Tanis, and your messengers have come as far as Hanes. All are confounded over a people that will not be able to profit them: they were not for help nor for any use, but for confusion and for reproach. LXX: Woe, you transgressing sons, says the Lord. You have taken counsel, and not through me; and a pact, not through my spirit, that you might add sins to sins: you who go to go down into Egypt, and have not asked me, that you may receive help from Pharaoh and be protected by the Egyptians. The protection of Pharaoh shall be to you for confusion, and to those who trust in Egypt, a reproach. For there are in Tanis princes, most evil messengers. In vain shall they labor for a people that will not profit them for help, nor for use, but for confusion and reproach. After the prophecy against Ariel, and the other things that the preceding discourse set forth up to this place, there now begins another prophecy, which is shown to have been fulfilled after the hundred and fifty years that lay between Isaiah and Jeremiah. For it foretells that history which we read in the volume of Jeremiah (Jer 41), when, Jerusalem having been overthrown and all its wealth and princes carried off to Babylon, Gedaliah son of Ahikam was set over those of royal stock who had remained in Judea; and when he had been slain by treachery together with his Chaldean companions, all the captains of the warriors, and Johanan son of Kareah, and Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah, and the rest of the common people from the least to the greatest, came to Jeremiah the prophet and said to him: Let our prayer fall before you, and pray for us to the Lord your God for all this remnant. For we are left a few out of many, as your eyes behold us; and let the Lord your God show us the way by which we should go, and the thing that we should do (Jer 42:2-3). And when Jeremiah, after ten days, had answered from the word of the Lord: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: If you remain quietly in this land, I will build you up and not pull you down, I will plant you and not pluck you up, for I am appeased concerning the evil that I have done to you. Do not be afraid of the face of the king of Babylon, whom you fearfully dread (ibid., 10-11). And a little after: But if you say: We will not dwell in this land; and set your face to enter Egypt, and go in to dwell there, the sword which you dread shall overtake you there, and the famine about which you are anxious shall cleave to you in Egypt, and there you shall die (ibid., 42:13, 15, 16). The proud men answered, saying to Jeremiah: You are speaking a lie: the Lord our God has not sent you, saying: Do not enter into Egypt to dwell there; but Baruch son of Neriah is inciting you against us, to deliver us into the hands of the Chaldeans, to kill us and to have us carried away to Babylon (Jer 43:2-3). At length all the princes of the people, gathering the remnant with the women and little ones and the king's daughters, not hearing the voice of the Lord, entered Egypt, taking Jeremiah and Baruch with them, and came to Tahpanhes, so that Jeremiah, as a sign of the captivity to come, prophesied against the disobedient people the things contained in his book. What, therefore, was to happen afterward is foretold many years before; and those are called deserting and transgressing sons who, forsaking the counsel of God which they had received through Jeremiah, followed their own will, and wove a web, not by the spirit of God, which sounded to them from the mouth of Jeremiah. He put the weaving of a web μεταφορικῶς, to show an evil counsel; and they did this so as to increase their former sins with the sin of contention and pride.

In this are reproved certain ones who wish to be governed by their own knowledge; of whom Isaiah says: 'Woe to you, deserting children! That you would take counsel and not from me, and would begin a web and not through my Spirit.' They weave spider's webs who cite sacred Scripture for evil purposes. Bernard says: 'You will never understand Paul unless you find the spirit of Paul.'

667. Woe to you, apostate children. In this part, the prophet threatens against those who despised the prophet Jeremiah, and who went into Egypt against his counsel, as it says in Jeremiah 42 and 43. And this is divided into two parts:

in the first, he threatens against the Jews only;

in the second, against the Jews together with the Egyptians, in whom they trusted, woe to them that go down (ch. 31).

Or, according to the Gloss,

in the first part, he prohibits them from descending to Egypt,

in the second, he threatens punishment against those who descend.

The first of these is divided into two:

in the first, he sets out threatening;

in the second, consolation: therefore the Lord waits (Isa 30:18).

The first of these is divided into two:

in the first, he denounces their descent;

in the second, he denounces their contempt of the divine command: therefore have I cried (Isa 30:7).

668. Concerning the first, he denounces three things in them.

First, the disposition of the journey, setting out the intention: that you would take counsel; a web, wicked machination; and the consequent effect: that you might add sin upon sin: why will you add sin upon sin? (2 Chr 28:13).

You who go down, he says, into Egypt, and have not asked my mouth. Not that they did not ask, but that they would not hear the counsel of the prophet, hoping for help in the strength of Pharaoh, and having confidence in the protection, or shadow, of Egypt. For the strength of Pharaoh, which is put twice in this place, the Hebrew has written MAOZ (מעוז). We have noted this so that, where we read in the last vision of Daniel (Dan 11) the God MAOZIM (מעוזים), we may understand not, as Porphyry dreams, the God of the village of Modim, but the mighty and strong God. Pharaoh among the Egyptians is the name of the royal power; and each is called by a particular name as well, as Pharaoh Neco and Pharaoh Hophra: as if we were to set Caesars and Augusti before the proper names of kings. And the strength of Pharaoh, he says, shall be to you for confusion, and the confidence in the shadow of Egypt for disgrace. The same Jeremiah writes that in Tahpanhes, a city of Egypt, he buried stones in the gate of Pharaoh's house, and said to the men of Judah: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, my servant, and I will set his throne upon these stones which I have hidden, and he shall set his throne upon them. And he shall come and strike the land of Egypt: such as are for death, to death; and such as are for captivity, to captivity; and such as are for the sword, to the sword: and he shall kindle a fire in the shrines of the gods of Egypt, and burn them, and carry them away captive. And he shall wrap himself in the land of Egypt as a shepherd wraps himself in his cloak, and he shall go forth from there in peace (Jer 43:10-12). For when the Egyptians had been overcome, the Jews too who had fled to the Egyptians were taken captive.

Scripture is the mouth of God. Hence Isaiah: "Woe to you who walk to go down into Egypt," that is, to secular sciences, "and have not asked at My mouth," that is, Sacred Scripture. We need not go down to other sciences in order to gain certainty before having had the witness on the mountain, that is, of Christ, Elias and Moses, meaning of the New Testament, of the Prophets and of the Law.

669. Second, he sets out the execution of this counsel as to walking the way: who walk, which is deformed by contempt of divine counsel; who have not asked at my mouth, the prophet: if you will separate the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth (Jer 15:19), because you would not do what he said; and by trusting in human help, trusting in the shadow of Egypt: cursed be the man that trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm (Jer 17:5).
And he sets out the effect: and the strength of Pharaoh shall be to your confusion: I will change their glory into shame (Hos 4:7).

And what follows: For your princes shall be in Tanis, and your messengers have come as far as Hanes, is to be read with mockery and ἐμφατικῶς: that, despising the counsel of God, they sent their princes to Tanis, a city of Egypt, in which was the royal house of Pharaoh, and where under Moses very many signs and portents were performed, as the Psalmist says: Who did wonders in the land of Egypt, in the plain of Tanis (Ps 77 [78]:43). And the same Isaiah says against Egypt: Where now are your wise men? Let them tell you and say what the Lord Sabaoth has purposed against Egypt. The princes of Tanis have failed (Isa 19:12-13); and he records that they failed at that time when the Lord entered Egypt upon a light cloud. We do not read of Hanes, a city of Egypt, anywhere else; but from his saying: Your messengers have come as far as Hanes, we understand that it is the farthest city of Egypt, toward the Ethiopians and the Blemmyes; for which the Seventy translated: Most evil messengers shall labor in vain, who trusted in the people of Egypt, which could not profit them, and they became an everlasting reproach.

Hence, as to the end of the way: for your princes went into Taphnis, which is only in the other part of Egypt, as if they feared to remain in the first borders: what have you to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the troubled water? (Jer 2:18).
And he shows their lack of hope: they were all confounded: put not your trust in princes: in the children of men, in whom there is no salvation (Ps 145:2–3[146:3]).

It is written in Isaiah: "the vision of the quadrupeds in tribulation and distress", and the rest, up to the place where he says: "the riches of the asps will not profit them". Let each one of us consider how great wealth of asps he has borne before this, how great riches of beasts, and how a rational man never sat upon our donkey — not the word of Moses, not of Isaiah, not of Jeremiah, nor of all the rest of the prophets — and he will see that the word of God and reason then sat upon us, when the Lord Jesus came and commanded his disciples that, going, they should untie "the colt of a donkey", which before had been tied up, so that it might walk free.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 37

But if you wish to learn yet more beasts, the prophet Isaiah will teach you, who, under "the vision" which he entitled "of the quadrupeds in the desert", speaks by the prophetic spirit certain such things concerning beasts: "in tribulation", he says, "and anguish, the lion and the lion's whelp; thence also the offspring of flying asps, who carried upon asses and camels their riches to a nation which shall not profit them". Can these things in any way be seen as said of bodily beasts, even by those who are exceedingly friends of the letter? For how can "the lion and the lion's whelp" or "the flying asps" "carry upon camels and asses their riches"? But evidently the prophet, filled with the Holy Spirit, enumerates the contrary powers of the most wicked demons, and designated that they place "the riches" of their deceptions upon souls stolid and perverse, which by a figure he compares to camels and asses. And that his soul might not be handed over to these beasts, fearing God he prayed, saying: "deliver not to the beasts the soul that confesses to you".

The burden of the beasts of the South. For this the Hebrew says MASSA BEEMOTH NEGEB (משא בהמות נגב), which the Seventy translated: The vision of the four-footed beasts in the desert. The foregoing exposition, which we have woven with a very full unfolding of the history, is the interpretation of this place: that, according to prophetic custom, the burden, that is, the weight and load of torments and punishments, came not only upon Babylon and Philistia, and Moab, and Damascus, and Egypt, and the desert of the sea, and also Edom and Arabia, and the valley of Zion, and lastly Tyre, but also upon the beasts of the South, which the Seventy translated four-footed beasts in the desert. He means the tribe of Judah, which, situated in the southern part, borders on the wilderness; and those who, rejecting the prophecy of Jeremiah, when Jerusalem had been taken, would not dwell in Judea, but fled through the desert to the Egyptians. And rightly are they called beasts of the South, or four-footed beasts in the desert, because they rejected the knowledge of God, and, despising his command, fled to the images of Egypt, having hope in Pharaoh; and whoever leans on him is like one who rests upon a reed, which, when broken, wounds the hand of him who leans on it. Of such beasts the sons of Korah too spoke in the psalm: Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he has been compared to the senseless beasts, and has become like them (Ps 48 [49]:13). And what follows: This way of theirs is a stumbling block to them, can rightly be understood of the present chapter: that the way of the desert was their ruin. I know that I have read that the beasts of the South and the four-footed beasts in the desert, who, leaving the borders of Judea, fled to the darkness of Egypt, refer to the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, and the rulers of this darkness, who through their longing for Egypt lost all their riches and former wealth. So he may have said. We, according to tropology, so as to discuss what we have not yet set out, say that all who, having deserted the Creator, have given themselves to the errors of the world are four-footed beasts in the desert of this world, from which they hope for help in vain, since they have abandoned the true help of God.

In a land of tribulation and anguish, the lioness and the lion: from them the viper and the flying basilisk: carrying their riches on the shoulders of beasts of burden, and their treasures on the hump of camels, to a people that will not be able to profit them: Egypt shall help in vain and to no purpose. LXX: In tribulation and anguish, the lion and the lion's whelp: thence asps and the offspring of flying asps: who carried their riches on asses and camels to a nation that will not profit them: the Egyptians will profit you emptily and vainly. For lion the Hebrew has written LEIS (ליש); and for flying basilisk, which the Seventy translated offspring of flying asps, in the Hebrew it is called ἐμπρηστὴς and flying, which we can call the burner, and in Hebrew it is named SARAPH (שרף). Again, in the place where we translated carrying on the shoulders of beasts of burden, for beasts of burden all alike translated πώλους, that is, the foals of asses. The land of tribulation and anguish signifies the vast waste of the wilderness, through which the remnant of Jerusalem, with Johanan son of Kareah and the daughters of King Zedekiah, taking with them all they could have, fled over to Egypt. Understand the lioness and the lion's whelp μεταφορικῶς as Jerusalem and its people, as Balaam says in Numbers: Behold, the people shall rise up as a lioness, and shall be lifted up as a lion: it shall not lie down until it devours the prey and drinks the blood of the slain (Num 23:24). In Ezekiel too it is written: Take up a lamentation for the prince of Israel, and say: Why did your mother, a lioness, lie down among lions, and rear her whelps in the midst of young lions (Ezek 19:1-2)? And lest we should think that holy Scripture speaks truly of a lioness and a lion, it speaks against the nature of things, saying that from a lioness and a lion was born a viper and a flying basilisk, or the flying offspring of asps: namely, that from evil parents worse children were begotten, of whom the Gospel too spoke: Brood of vipers, who showed you to flee from the wrath to come (Matt 3:7)? And to the land of Israel it is said: You are a land on which it has not rained, nor has a shower come upon you in the day of wrath; whose princes in the midst of it are like roaring lions, seizing the prey, devouring souls by their might (Ezek 22:24-25). These offspring of vipers, or of flying asps, that is, the princes of the people and the whole crowd of the ungodly, went to a people that could not profit them, as Jeremiah says (Jer 44), that the Lord would deliver Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies and into the hands of those who sought his life, and that all the men of Judah who were in the land of Egypt would be consumed by sword and famine to utter destruction; so much so that the Hebrews hand down that, before Nebuchadnezzar took Egypt, Jeremiah and Baruch escaped the impending captivity by death. A certain writer expounded the lioness and the lion's whelp as the heavenly Jerusalem and the people deceived from it; and the flying basilisk, and the vipers, and the offspring of asps, as that crooked serpent of which we read above (above, Isa 14 and 27), and of which the Savior spoke in the Gospel: I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18): who, called a dragon in the Apocalypse (Rev 12), drew down with him to the earth a third part of the stars, which by the perversity of their judgment lost their former riches, abandoning them in the Egypt of this world.

670. Third, he describes the carrying away of goods: the burden of the beasts;

he threatens first the destruction of Egypt. The burden, of the sons of Judah, beasts, because of their stupidity or because they bore their goods like beasts; of the south, because they fled to the south or because their dwelling was in the southern part. In a land of trouble, in Egypt, which in Hebrew is called "Meyrey," which is translated "trouble" or "distress": the sword which you fear, shall overtake you there in the land of Egypt (Jer 42:16).

Second, he sets out the condition of those who carry away the goods: the lioness, because of its ferocity, the lion, because of the presumption of its audacity, the viper, because of its cruelty, the flying basilisk, not because it has wings, but because it leaps on the face of men, because of its swiftness to do evil: her princes are as roaring lions (Zeph 3:3).

Third, the carrying away of the goods: they carry their riches.

Fourth, the vanity of their labor: to a people that shall not be able to profit them: vain is the salvation of man (Ps 59:13[60:11]).

Therefore I have cried out concerning this: it is only pride: be still. For which the Seventy translators, meaning I know not what, translated: Announce these things, since this consolation of yours is vain. Further, Symmachus translated ταραχαί εἰσιν κατοικεῖν, that is, there are tumults, that they may dwell. The Hebrew word REEB (רהב) Aquila translated ὅρμημα, that is, onset and pride; Symmachus disturbance; the Seventy vanity; Theodotion breadth; it is written with three letters, RES and HE and BETH, and it is the very word read in the Psalms: I will be mindful of Rahab and of Babylon, who know me (Ps 86 [87]:4). And the sense is: Since in the Egyptians there is vain help, I have commanded her, that is, Jerusalem, or I have cried out, that the Egyptians had only the name of a kingdom, and pride without strength; and that Israel ought to sit or dwell in its own land, and not seek help in vain from the weak.

[Isaiah] set his prophecy down in writing in a new book so that, after his prophecy was fulfilled, what he had written might bear witness against the Jews of what the inspired prophet predicted to them a long time before. This is why he did not simply write it in a book, but in a new book, a book capable of staying sturdy for a long time without easily falling apart, a book which could last until the events described in it would come to pass.

Now go in and write for them on boxwood, and inscribe it carefully in a book: and it shall be in the last day for a testimony forever. The Hebrews say that, since in the prophets there is one spirit, and all times are joined together with the Lord, Jeremiah is commanded, and it is God's charge, that, having entered Egypt, he should write for them on boxwood, which is a wood that does not rot; or, as Symmachus translated, ἐπὶ πτυχὶ, that is, on a very broad tablet. For them, doubtless for the Jews: and that he should set it out carefully in a book, so that there may be no difficulty in reading it, so that when the prophecy has been fulfilled in fact, they may then understand that the word of the prophets is true. We run over the plain things so that we may linger on the more obscure.

Second, he sets out the confirmation of the command. Now therefore, you, Isaiah, go in, by prophetic vision, or you, Jeremiah, go in, into Egypt with the people, as it says in Jeremiah 43;

third, he assigns the fruit of this confirmation: and it shall be in that day for a testimony for ever: write this for a memorial (Exod 17:14).

For it is a people provoking to anger, and lying sons, sons unwilling to hear the law of God. Who say to the seers: Do not see; and to those who look: Do not look out for us the things that are right: speak to us pleasing things; see errors for us. Take the way away from me: turn the path aside from me: let the Holy One of Israel cease from before our face. It is plain that they provoked the Lord to anger, unwilling to hear the words of Jeremiah (Jer 43). They said to him: Do not see for us what we do not want: do not forbid us the way of Egypt, nor preach the things that are right; but say what pleases us, that we may go on into Egypt, which heaps sins upon sins. Why do you press upon us what we do not willingly hear? why do you show the way by which we do not wish to go? Why do you so often repeat in our ears: Thus says the Lord, the Holy One of Israel? Let this preaching cease from us. According to tropology, all heretics are called lying sons. For they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2); they do not hear the Law of God with the ears of the inner man, and they say to the teachers of the Churches: Do not see for us the things that are right, nor threaten the flames of Gehenna; but promise us the kingdom of heaven, so that after luxury and delights paradise may be opened to us. Why do you show me the way of the Lord, by which I do not willingly go? Why do you repeat the name of the Holy One of Israel, or the word of Israel, which does not penetrate the secret places of my breast? This indeed is said also to the people of the Church when it is negligent, if it turns away from the severity of its teachers and favors flatterers.

673. For it is a people. Here he sets out the contempt of the people,

and first, the contempt by which they despised God: that provokes to wrath, as to sin of transgression: do not you provoke me, as the house of Israel provokes me (Ezek 2:8); and lying children, as to sin of speech, for they promised obedience to Jeremiah, a promise which they would not keep, as it says in Jeremiah 42. The children that are strangers have lied to me (Ps 17:46[18:45]): that will not, as to sin of omission: he that stops his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be an abomination (Prov 28:9).

The chief priests and the Pharisees, through the agency of Pilate, sealed the tomb; but the women saw him who was risen.… The chief priests lacked understanding, but the women beheld with their own eyes.
