Further, what follows: Blessed is he who has seed in Zion, and kinsmen in Jerusalem, we can interpret so as to say that it fits the sense of the present passage, in that the divine word exhorts those fleeing into Egypt to return to Jerusalem and beget sons. To this city so great a blessedness is promised that it is defended and protected by the help of the Lord; and in another place it is written of it: The glory of this latter house will be greater than that of the former (Hag 2:10). This can also be referred to the Church, the vision of peace and the watchtower, of which it is written: Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God (Ps 86 [87]:2). And elsewhere: The rush of the river makes glad the city of God (ibid. 45 [46]:3). For in her is the fire and the furnace, to devour sinners and to consume wood, hay and stubble; or the light and the oven, so that the brightness of the righteous and the punishment of sinners may be shown.

Of this love that is begun here to be perfected from the sight of the Lord in the eternal kingdom Isaiah rightly speaks, saying, "The Lord lives, whose fire is in Zion, and his furnace in Jerusalem." It is, however, greater to be a furnace than a fire because a fire can also be small, but a larger flame is kindled in a furnace. Zion truly is said to be speculation but Jerusalem the vision of peace. Truly we sometimes catch a glimpse of our peace here in order there later to see it fully. Therefore through the Lord's love the fire is in Zion and his furnace in Jerusalem because here we burn in some measure with the flames of his love when we glimpse him, but there we shall burn totally when we shall fully see him whom we love.

If the breads of the furnace that were baked in secret signify the interior devotion of the mind of the faithful confirmed by the fire of charity, breads which were also commanded by the law to be offered in the sacrifice of the Lord, it is most fitting that the hearts which were made to burn constantly with the flame of intimate love and virtue and to beget words are symbolized through the furnaces in which the same breads were baked. The prophet spoke beautifully about these things when he referred to "the Lord whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem." It is also written: "Did our hearts not burn within us when he spoke along the way and opened the Scriptures to us?"

The precept of the law, therefore, is to be taken in a more spiritual sense. For there is spiritual seed which is conceived through the love and fear of God in the spiritual womb, travailing and bringing forth the spirit of salvation. And in this sense must be understood this verse: Blessed is he who hath seed in Zion and posterity in Jerusalem. For does it mean that, although he be a whoremonger and a drunkard and an idolater, he is still blessed if only he hath seed in Sion and posterity in Jerusalem? No one in his senses will say this.
An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 4, Chapter 24

But if you ask how these things come about, ask grace, not doctrine; desire, not understanding; the groaning of prayer, not the study of reading; the Bridegroom, not the master; God, not man; darkness, not clarity; not light, but the fire that wholly inflames and carries into God through ecstatic anointings and most ardent affections. Which fire is indeed God, and his furnace is in Jerusalem, and Christ kindles this in the fervor of his most ardent passion, which only he truly perceives who says: My soul has chosen hanging, and my bones death. Whoever loves this death can see God, because it is indubitably true: No man shall see me and live. Let us die, therefore, and enter into the darkness; let us impose silence upon our cares, concupiscences, and phantasms; let us pass over with Christ crucified from this world to the Father, so that, when the Father is shown to us, we may say with Philip: It suffices us; let us hear with Paul: My grace suffices for you; let us exult with David, saying: My flesh and my heart have failed, God of my heart and God my portion forever. Blessed be the Lord forever, and let all the people say: So be it, so be it. Amen.

697. Third, he sets out the strengthening of both: the Lord has said it, whose fire, burning the Assyrians, above: the light of Israel shall be as a fire, and the Holy One thereof as a flame (Isa 10:17); or the fire on the altar of incense; his furnace, on the altar of holocausts: the fire on the altar shall always burn (Lev 6:12); or the fire of charity burning imperfectly in the Church militant, but a furnace burning perfectly in the Church triumphant.

698. Note also that charity is called a fire: see the collation preceding this chapter.
32: These things are according to the Hebrew, from which the Seventy disagree in most places not only in words but also in senses. For when the righteous king has reigned, and his princes have ruled with judgment, there will be a man hiding his words, a man who by nature is God, and he will hide his words, speaking to them in parables (Matt 20:21, 23, 24, and 25). And he will hide them as from running water, that is, from the people of the Jews, which, like water, is borne and drawn this way and that at the will of its teachers. This man, hiding his words among the unbelieving, will appear in Zion, that is, in the Church, like a glorious river running down in a thirsty land. For he will appear to the people of the Gentiles, which before suffered thirst for the truth; and the river of God will water the thirsty fields, the river of which it is written: The rush of the river makes glad the city of God (Ps 45 [46]:4). And in another place: The river of God is filled with waters (Ps 64 [65]:10). For he himself says in the Gospel: He who thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as the Scripture says, out of his belly will flow rivers of living water (John 7:38). Then they will by no means have confidence in their teachers, but will offer their ears to hear the Lord; and both with heart and with tongue they will confess the peace of the Lord, forsaking the foolish princes and their ministers, who imposed silence on those who believed in Jesus.

Behold, a king will reign with righteousness, and princes will rule in judgment. And a man will be like one who is hidden from the wind and conceals himself from the tempest: like streams of waters in thirst, and the shade of a jutting rock in a desert land. The eyes of those who see will not be dimmed, and the ears of those who hear will listen diligently. And the heart of the foolish will understand knowledge, and the tongue of stammerers will speak quickly and plainly. He who is senseless will no longer be called a prince, nor will the deceitful man be called great. For the fool will speak foolish things, and his heart will work iniquity, to accomplish pretense, and to speak deceitfully to the Lord, and to empty the soul of the hungry, and to take away drink from the thirsty. The vessels of the deceitful man are most evil: for he has devised schemes to destroy the meek with the word of a lie, when the poor man spoke judgment. But the prince will think the things that are worthy of a prince, and he himself will stand over the leaders. LXX: For behold, a righteous king will reign, and princes will rule with judgment. And there will be a man hiding his words, and he will be hidden as from water that is borne along: and he will appear in Zion like a running river, glorious in a thirsty land; and they will by no means be trusting in men, but they will give their ears to hear, and the heart of the weak will attend to hearing, and the tongues of the stammering will quickly learn to speak peace: and they will no longer tell the fool to be a prince, nor will your ministers any longer say, Be silent. For the fool will speak foolish things, and his heart will understand vain things, to accomplish iniquity and to speak error to the Lord, to scatter the hungry souls and to make the thirsty souls empty. For the counsel of the most wicked will think unjust things: to slay the humble with unjust words, and to scatter the words of the humble in judgment. But the pious have thought wisdom, and this counsel abides. According to the Seventy Translators, who said: For behold, a righteous king will reign, and princes will rule with judgment, what follows must be joined to what precedes, namely to the words with which the previous section ended: Blessed is he who has seed in Zion, and kinsmen in Jerusalem. According to the Hebrew, the former prophecy, concerning those who were going down into Egypt, is finished, and now begins another oracle, namely concerning the coming of Christ and of his Apostles. For this king will reign righteously, not respecting persons in judgment, and his princes will rule with truth, considering causes, not men.

This is the third part of the threatening, in which he describes their liberation from the enemies who were threatening them then. And first, he foretells the liberation in the manner of prophecy, second, he recounts it in the manner of history: and it came to pass (ch. 36). The first of these is divided into two parts: in the first, he foretells the prosperity of the Jews; in the second, the destruction of their enemies: woe to you that spoils (ch. 33).

Concerning the first, he does two things. First, he foretells the status of the liberated, as to the equity of the king: a king shall reign, namely, Ezechias: a king shall reign, and shall be wise (Jer 23:5); as to the prosperity of the people: and princes shall rule in judgment.

And whoever is under his shelter will be as safe in tribulations and distresses, and in the tempest of this world, as one who, fleeing wind and whirlwind, hides himself in a safe place; and as one who finds the purest springs in the desert; and as one who, in fierce heat, when the blaze of the sun scorches everything, rests under a jutting rock. Where we said: like streams of waters in thirst, the Seventy translated: and he will appear in Zion like a running river. For the Hebrew word about which we argued above, BASAION (בציון), which means in thirst, or in dryness, and in a pathless place, the Seventy and Theodotion translated in Zion, reading SION, which is written with the same letters, for SAION, that is, thirst.
As to consolation in tribulation: and a man shall be as when one is hid from the wind, above: there shall be a tabernacle for a shade in the daytime from the heat (Isa 4:6).

When, therefore, Christ has reigned, and his princes have ruled in judgment, the eyes of those who believe will not be dimmed, and the ears of those who hear, which before were deaf, will attend diligently, and the heart of those once foolish will understand knowledge, and the tongue of the stammering and the mute, which could not utter Christ, will confess the Lord with full and open speech.

As to amendment in spiritual matters: the eyes of them that see, namely, the prophets, shall not be dim, as before, because of the sins of the king and the people, but shall receive clear visions from the Lord; and the ears, namely, of their subjects, shall hearken, fulfilling the precepts of the Lord given by the prophets.

The heart of fools, who formerly erred following idols; and the tongue of stammerers, the prophets, who formerly spoke obscurely and enigmatically: wisdom opened the mouth of the dumb, and made the tongues of infants eloquent (Wis 10:21).

He who is foolish will no longer be called a prince (1 Cor 1). For God has made foolish the wisdom of this world. Nor will the deceitful and perverse teacher be called great among the peoples: namely the scribes and Pharisees, to whom the Lord said: Fools and blind, which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold? (Matt 23:17).

And also as to their consequent liberty, namely, from tyrants: the fool shall no more be called prince, namely, Sennacherib, to whom formerly they paid tribute, as is evident in 2 Kings 18:14. I will deliver them out of the hand of the king of the Assyrians (Ezek 24).

What follows contains nearly the same sense as the Hebrew, and can be fitted to the heretics. For these speak a lie against the Lord, and pervert the hungry and thirsty souls, and make them go away empty; so that even if they have anything good by nature, they lose it through the fault of their teachers, whose whole counsel is to destroy the humble with unjust words and to scatter the words of the humble in judgment. In which it must likewise be noted that whoever can be deceived by them is humble, and clings to the earth.

For the fool will speak foolish things, for which in the Hebrew it is written: NABAL NABALA IDABBER (נבל נבלה ידבר). We say this in order to explain the words of Abigail, who says of Nabal the Carmelite: According to his name he is foolish (1 Sam 25:25). For truly the fool will speak foolish things, and his heart will accomplish iniquity: he who feared where there was no fear, and practiced folly in place of wisdom, saying: If this man were from God, he would not break the sabbath (John 9:16). This the master of the synagogues does to this day, to accomplish pretense, for which in the Hebrew is written ONEPH (חנף), that is, ὑπόκρισις. Hence it is said again and again to the Pharisees: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites (Matt 23:14). And he will speak, he says, deceitfully to the Lord: Master, we know that you are from God, and that you have no concern for men; is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not? (ibid. 22:16, 17). They empty the souls of the hungry people, and take away drink from the thirsty crowds, neither entering themselves nor allowing others to enter.

And they [our opponents] even joined in censuring us, as if we thought the opposite to the things that we have already written. But I learn that they say this also, namely, that recently we have accepted a doctrinal statement, or a new creed, perhaps, I suppose, because we lightly esteem the ancient and august one. "The fool will say foolish things, and his heart will think nonsense." However, we say this, that no individuals have demanded an explanation from us, nor have we accepted one newly coined by others. For the divinely inspired Scripture and the vigilance of our holy Fathers and the creed formulated by those who are in every way orthodox are sufficient for us.

Second, he describes the manner of liberation: for the fool. And first, he describes the affliction; second, the liberation: until the spirit be poured upon us (Isa 32:15). Concerning the first, he does two things: first, he describes the enemy who persecutes them; second, the persecution: rise up, you rich women (Isa 32:9). Concerning the first, he sets out three things. First, the wickedness of the king himself, as to the blasphemy of his mouth: the fool, namely, Sennacherib, will speak foolish things, blasphemous words, below (Isa 37:17). The mouth of fools bubbles out folly (Prov 15:2); as to the duplicity of his heart: his heart will work iniquity, promising good land to the people, to the Lord deceitfully, saying he has come by his command, below (Isa 36:10). The thoughts of the just are counsels (Prov 12:5); as to the cruelty of his work: to make empty the soul of the hungry, despoiling them of the things by which they ought to have been nourished, against what it says in Proverbs 25:21: if your enemy be hungry, give him to eat.

For all the vessels and weapons of the deceitful teacher and prince are most evil; he contrives snares to destroy the simple with the word of a lie, saying to the deceived people: Search and see, that a prophet does not arise from Galilee (John 7:52). When the poor man spoke to them judgment: he who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake (2 Cor 8). For truly Christ spoke judgment and righteousness to them, saying: If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me: but if I do them, even if you will not believe me, believe the works (John 10:37).

Second, the malice of his princes: the vessels, that is, the messengers and princes, of the deceitful, namely, of Sennacherib: a prince that gladly hears lying words, has all his servants wicked (Prov 29:12); and the execution of their malice: for he, namely, Rabsaces, about whom, see below (36), will frame (concinnabit), that is, compose, devices—cinnus is a kind of drink composed of different kinds of things; the poor man, the Jew: your mouth has abounded with evil, and your tongue framed deceits (Ps 49[50]:19).

This poor man who speaks judgment, the prince and Lord, will think the things that are worthy of a prince, saying: I came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 15:24). And he will be anxious for the unbelieving, desiring to save those who do not believe; and he will stand over his leaders, the Apostles, to one of whom he says: But you, a man of one mind with me, my leader and my familiar friend (Ps 54 [55]:14).
Third, the prudence of Ezechias in his reign: the prince, for Ezechias commanded that no one should respond to Sennacherib, above: I will restore your princes as they were before (Isa 1:26).

After the calling of the nations, when Christ the king has ruled with righteousness, and his princes, the Apostles and apostolic men, have presided over the believers with judgment, the prophetic word will be directed to the wealthy women, whom we must take either as the cities of Judea, or as the synagogues of that time, or, as most think, as the matrons of the rich men of the former people of the Jews, to whom, as to women lying prostrate after their ruin, it is said: Rise; and they are nonetheless called confident daughters, or hoping; and they are commanded to hear the words of the Lord, and to remember the days and the year, of which we shall speak in what follows, as the Savior himself says: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me: he has sent me to preach the gospel to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives and sight to the blind, to call the acceptable year of the Lord (Luke 4:18, 19); and that this very remembrance may become for them, according to the Seventy, grief with hope, so that they may lament that they denied the Lord, and may have hope of salvation if they repent. For he says that the vintage is ended, and that after the last devastation, which happened under Vespasian and Titus and Hadrian, no other captivity will come, nor will clusters remain among the peoples to be gathered afterward.

Here he describes the persecution inflicted on them as to three things. First, as to the loss of fruits, stirring up attention: you women, who cry easily, rich, who have reason to cry from the ruin of their goods; or you women, that is, you feeble Jews: they that trust in their own strength, and glory in the multitude of their riches (Ps 48:7[49:6]).

And he sets out the determination of the time: after several days and one year: for tribulation is very near: for there is none to help me (Ps 21:12[22:11]). And he sets out the loss of fruits: the vintage is at an end, destroyed, the gathering, of crops, shall come no more, into our houses from the fields: the joy of the vintage is taken away (Jer 48:33).

Hence they are summoned to lamentation, and are commanded to bare their breasts and to gird their loins, because the country once desirable, and the fruitful vine, of which it is written: I planted you a fruitful vine, wholly true: how have you turned into the bitterness of a strange vine? (Jer 2:21), has been destroyed by the ravaging Roman.
Second, as to the devastation of the fields, he prescribes mourning, be astonished: I have put off the robe of peace (Bar 4:20), above: and the Lord in that day shall call to weeping (Isa 22:12).
And he foretells harm: upon the land, above: briers and thorns shall come up (Isa 5:6) over it.

Over the ground, he says, of my people thorns and briers, or grass will come up. And the sense is: if thorns and briers have filled the land of Judea, which is the land of promise, how much more the other cities, which are full of joy, and which that saying of the Gospel will overtake: Woe to you who rejoice now, for you will weep (Luke 6:25)!

What was said above according to the LXX: Over the land of my people thorns and grass will come up, can be referred both to the heretics and to all the simple among believers, who do not understand Holy Scripture as befits its majesty. Hence we have fitted each to each: that the land of the people of God brings forth thorns for the heretics, and grass for all the unskilled in the Church.

If those very persons, who amid the darkness of the present life shine bright by virtuous attainments—if they also cannot be void of contagion, with what guilt of wickedness are those bound, who still live after the flesh? If those persons cannot be free from sin who are already walking in the way of heavenly desires, what about those who still lie under the loads of sinful habits, who, abandoned to the gratifications of their fleshly part, still bear the yoke of rottenness? So Peter says, "And if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?" And it is said by Isaiah, "Upon the land of my people shall come up thorns and briars; how much more upon all the houses of joy in the joyous city." The "house of joy in the joyous city" is the mind of the wicked, which neglects to regard the punishments that are destined to come, in the gratification of the flesh, and going away from itself, it revels in empty mirth.
Morals on the Book of Job 17.23

Third, as to the desolation of their cities and houses, he sets out the desolation itself: how much more, namely, to be wept for, the city that rejoiced, namely, Jerusalem, whose lower part was handed over to the Assyrians, above: a populous city, a joyous city (Isa 22:2).

Wealthy women, rise and hear my voice: confident daughters, take in my speech with your ears. After days and a year you too will be troubled, you confident ones: for the vintage is ended; the gathering will come no more. Be astonished, you wealthy women; be troubled, you confident ones: strip yourselves and be confounded. For which Symmachus translated be made naked; there follows: Gird your loins, lament upon your breasts, over the desirable country, over the fruitful vine: thorns and briers will come up over the ground of my people: how much more over all the houses of joy of the exulting city? For the house has been forsaken; the multitude of the city has been left; darkness and groping have come upon the caves for ever: the joy of wild asses, pastures of flocks. Until the spirit is poured out upon us from on high: and the desert will be in Carmel, and Carmel will be counted as a forest. And judgment will dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness will sit in Carmel. And the work of righteousness will be peace, and the service of righteousness silence, and security for ever. And my people will sit in the beauty of peace, and in the tabernacles of confidence, and in wealthy rest. But hail in the descent of the forest, and the city will be brought low with lowliness. Blessed are you who sow upon all waters, sending forth the foot of the ox and the ass. The LXX, for the darkness and groping which have come upon the caves for ever, translated and your villages will be caves for ever: what in the Hebrew is called OPHEL (עפל) and BEEN (בחן), which the Hebrews think were two towers in Jerusalem, lofty and very strong, called by these names. The first of them means darkness, or cloud, because it raised its head up to the clouds; the other, proving and firmness, or, as Symmachus renders it, inquiry: because the eyes were deceived in gazing at its summit.

For the Lord, that is, my temple, has been forsaken, as I said to the Apostles: Rise, let us go hence (John 14:31); and to the unbelieving: Your house will be left to you desolate (Luke 13:35). Palpable darkness has taken possession of the inner sanctuaries of the Temple and its secret mysteries, and they have become no longer storerooms for the vessels of the Lord, but caves for ever. For they had heard from the Lord Savior (Matt 21:13): The house of my Father shall be called a house of prayer: but you have made it a den of robbers. The joy, he says, of wild asses, pastures of flocks. This is to be understood either according to the letter, in that all things are deserted; or spiritually, in that, Israel having been driven out, savage men who have no knowledge of God dwell in Judea.

And the magnitude of the desolation as to the houses, for they were reduced to perpetual darkness, as happens to ruined buildings: and darkness: they shall grope in the dark, and not in the light (Job 12:25); and as to their fields: a joy of wild asses, which dwell in great wildernesses: a wild ass accustomed to the wilderness (Jer 2:24).

And this is to be until the spirit is poured out upon us from on high, which the Savior, ascending to the Father, promised to believers, saying: Behold, I go, and I will send you the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth (John 16). And again: Until you receive power from on high (Luke 24:49). And what he had said above: Yet a little while, and Lebanon will be in Carmel, and Carmel will be counted as a forest: and in that day the deaf will hear the words of the book, and out of darkness and gloom the eyes of the blind will see (above, Isa 29), he now repeats in other words: that the wilderness of the nations is turned into the riches of Israel, and Israel is counted among the nations: at which time judgment will have dwelt in the desert, the Lord and Savior, to whom the Father has given all judgment (John 3). And righteousness will rest in Carmel, of which it was said above: And the desert will be in Carmel: that judgment and righteousness dwell in the desert, and rest in Carmel, which before was called the desert.

Here he describes their liberation. And first, he sets out the consolation of the Jews; second, the destruction of their enemies: but hail (Isa 32:19); third, the prophet's congratulation: blessed are you that sow (Isa 32:20). Concerning the first, he sets out three things. First, divine consolation: these things, I say, will happen, when Sennacherib lays waste the land, until the spirit, divine consolation, be poured upon us: you shall know that I am the Lord, for I will send spirit into you, and you shall live (Ezek 37:5–6).

Second, the manner and order of the consolation, as to the fertility of the land: and the desert shall be as Carmel, and Carmel shall be counted for a forest; that is, your land, formerly a desert, will be so fertile like Carmel, that Carmel's fertility will be considered barrenness in comparison to your land; above (Isa 29:19) has the same thing.
As the observation of justice: and judgment shall dwell, above: Zion shall be redeemed in judgment (Isa 1:27).

The work of righteousness too will be peace, which, according to the Apostle, surpasses all understanding (Phil 4). And the service of righteousness silence, so that they may worship the Lord not with the much speaking of the Jews but with the brevity of faith; and may rest secure in eternal peace, and in their tabernacles may be the riches of which the Apostle spoke (1 Cor 1:5): I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ, because in everything you have been made rich in him, in all speech and in all knowledge.

He that suffers from a flux of seed is pronounced unclean, because, being addicted to much speaking, he defiles himself by that which, had it been orderly issued, might have produced the offspring of right thought in the hearts of hearers; and, while he incautiously spends himself in loquacity, he sheds his seed not so as to serve for generation, but unto uncleanness.
The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part 2, Chapter 4

It is the practice of the impertinent ever to answer by the opposite what is said aright, lest, if they assent to the things asserted, they should seem inferior. And to these the words of the righteous, however small in number they have been heard, are 'much,' in that as they cut their evil habits to the quick, they fall heavy upon the hearing, whence that is even wrested to a crime, which by a right declaration is pronounced against crimes. For the very person, who had delivered strong sentences on grounds of truth, Zophar rebukes and calls full of words, in that, whereas wisdom reprimands sins by the mouth of the righteous, it sounds like superfluity of talkativeness to the ears of the foolish. For froward men account nothing right, but what they themselves think, and they reckon the words of the righteous idle in the degree that they find them differing from their own notions. Nor yet did Zophar deliver a fallacious sentiment, 'that a man full of words could never be justified,' in that so long as anyone lets himself out in words, the gravity of silence being gone, he parts with the safe keeping of the soul. For hence it is written, "And the work of righteousness, silence." Hence Solomon saith, "He that hath no rule over his own spirit in talking, is like a city that is broken down, and without walls." Hence he says again, "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin." Hence the Psalmist bears witness, saying, "Let not a man full of words be established upon the earth"; but the worth of a true sentence is lost, when it is not delivered under the keeping of discretion. Thus it is a certain truth, that 'a man full of words cannot be justified,' but a good thing is not well said, because there is no heed taken to whom it is spoken. For a true sentence against the wicked, if it is aimed at the virtue of the good, loses its own virtue, and bounds back with blunted point, in proportion as that is strong which it hits. But that the wicked cannot hear good words with patience, and that wherein they neglect the amending of their life, they brace themselves up to words of rejoinder, Zophar plainly instructs us.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 10, Section 2

And as to the tranquility of peace: and the work, that is, the effect, of justice shall be peace, and the service of justice quietness, for it will be without the tumult of contentions and wars, above: Lord, you will give us peace (Isa 26:12).

Note on the words, the work of justice shall be peace, that the peace of the saints in heaven will be beautiful, first, because it will not be false (Wis 15); second, because it will not be interrupted, above: and there shall be no end of peace (Isa 9:7); third, because it will be full: he has placed peace in your borders (Ps 147:14).

Note also on the peace to come that three things make it desirable: first, the strength of divine power: they that trust in the Lord shall be as mount Zion: he shall not be moved for ever that dwells in Jerusalem (Ps 124[125]:1–2); second, the purity of one's own conscience: you shall walk confidently in your way, and your foot shall not stumble (Prov 3:23); third, the removal of hostile wickedness: have confidence. I have overcome the world (John 16:33).

And when the Christian people sits, or dwells, in beauty, or, as the Seventy translated, in the city of peace, which is without doubt in the Church, then hail and tempest and the raging wrath of the Lord will come down upon the forest, of which it was said above: And Carmel will be counted as a forest; and the city of Jerusalem will be brought low, and, according to another Scripture, will speak from the earth.

Third, he sets out the pleasant enjoyment of divine consolation: and my people shall sit in the beauty of peace: but he that shall hear me, shall rest without terror, and shall enjoy abundance (Prov 1:33).
Hail, namely, of tribulation, in the descent of the forest, that is, it shall descend from the Lord upon your enemies; the city, Ninive, above: the high city he shall lay low (Isa 26:5).
The prophet says, "Blessed is he that sows into all waters, whose ox and donkey tread," [that is] the people, from the law and from the Gentiles, gathered into one faith.

Only let us not be condemned for frivolity by asking for little, and for what is unworthy of the giver. Blessed is he from whom Jesus asks drink, as he did from that Samaritan woman, and gives a well of water springing up unto eternal life. Blessed is he that sows beside all waters, and upon every soul, tomorrow to be ploughed and watered, which today the ox and the donkey tread, while it is dry and without water, and oppressed with lack of rationality. And blessed is he who, though he be a "valley of rushes," is watered out of the house of the Lord; for he is made fruit-bearing instead of rush-bearing and produces that which is for the food of man, not that which is rough and unprofitable. And for the sake of this we must be very careful not to miss the grace.

Accordingly, like a perfect man learned in the law and made firm in the gospel, accept the faith of both Testaments, for, as we read today, "Blessed is he who sows upon every water, where the ox and the donkey tread," that is, who sows upon the people who follow the teaching of both Testaments. This is the ploughman's ox, wearing the yoke of the law, of which the law says, "You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out your corn," for this ox has the horns of holy Scripture. But in the Gospel the Lord, representing the people of the Gentiles, mounts the colt of a donkey.

Let them take as much pleasure as they please in their Gallican geldings; we will be satisfied with the simple "donkey" of Zechariah, loosed from its halter and made ready for the Savior's service, which received the Lord on its back and so fulfilled Isaiah's prediction: "Blessed is he that sows beside all waters, where the ox and the donkey tread under foot."

Do we ask where we have read of the ox and the ass together? In Deuteronomy it is written: You shall not plough with a calf and an ass together (Deut 22:10). And in this same Isaiah: Blessed is he who sows upon every water, where the ox and the ass tread (Isa 32:20). Ebion ploughs with the ox and the ass together, worthy, for the lowliness of his understanding, of the poverty of his name; for he so receives the Gospel as not to abandon the ceremonies of the Jewish superstitions, which went before in shadow and image. But blessed is he who sows in the words of the Scriptures, of the old as well as of the new Instrument, and treads the waters of the letter that kills, so as to reap the fruit of the life-giving spirit.
At the end of the section too they translated thus: Blessed are those who sow upon every water, where the ox and the ass tread.

Since these things are so, and we have learned from the prophetic oracle how great the goods are that the Church will possess, and how great the evils that Jerusalem will suffer: blessed are you, Apostles, and you other teachers, who sow upon all the waters of Holy Scripture, in which the ox and the ass tread. The ox is a clean animal, on account of the election of the fathers; the ass unclean, on account of the former idolatry of the Gentiles; so that the Church of the Lord may be gathered both from the Circumcision and from the Uncircumcision.

By water peoples are denoted, as it is said by John, "Now the waters are peoples." By water likewise not only the tide of peoples drifting away, but also the minds of good men that follow the preachings of faith, are denoted, as the Prophet saith, "Blessed are ye that sow upon all waters." And it is said by the Psalmist; "The voice of the Lord is upon the waters."
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 19

What else is meant by 'seed,' but the word of preaching? As the Truth says in the Gospel, "A sower went forth to sow"; and as the Prophet says; "Blessed are ye who sow upon all waters." What else but the Church, ought to be understood by the threshing floor? Of which it is said by the voice of the Forerunner; "And He will throughly purge His floor."
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 31

Here he shows the prophet's congratulation: upon waters, that is, upon the places that are fertile from the abundance of the waters; sending thither the foot of the ox and the ass, not at the same time, for this was prohibited: you shall not plough with an ox and an ass together (Deut 22:10); for you shall eat the labors of your hands: blessed are you, and it shall be well with you (Ps 127[128]:2).

Note also on the words, blessed are you that sow upon waters, that the teaching of the Lord is water: first, because it abounds: I, wisdom, have poured out rivers (Sir 24:40); second, because it cools: as cold water to a thirsty soul (Prov 25:25); third, because it makes fruitful, below: as the rain comes down from heaven, and returns no more thither, but soaks the earth, and makes it to spring, so shall my word be, which shall go forth from my mouth (Isa 55:10–11); fourth, because it carries quickly: it shall become in him a fountain of water, springing up into life everlasting (John 4:14); fifth, because it conforms itself to each individually: in the streets divide your waters (Prov 5:16).
33: Woe to you who plunder: will you not yourself be plundered? And you who despise: will you not yourself be despised? When you have finished plundering, you will be plundered: when, wearied, you have ceased to scorn, you will be scorned. LXX: Woe to those who make you wretched: for no one makes you wretched. And those who reject you do not reject you: those who reject will be taken, and will be handed over, and like a moth in a garment so will they be overcome. He had spoken of the Apostles and of the teachers of the churches: Blessed are those who sow upon every water, where the ox and the ass tread: now he directs a curse at their persecutors, nay, at their prince, who possesses the hearts of the impious: that whatever they have done they may receive back, and their present power may be the material of future torments. Hence according to the LXX it is said: Woe to those who make you wretched: for no one makes you wretched. And the sense is: as far as lies in them, when they persecute you and afflict you with various tortures, they think you wretched once you have been killed and tortured. But no one can make you wretched, for they have power not over the soul, but over the body. And he who rejects you does not reject you, but him who sent you, according to what the Savior says to the disciples: He who rejects you rejects me: and he who rejects me rejects him who sent me (Luke 10:16). The persecutors, therefore, will be taken, and will be handed over to eternal fires. And as a moth consumes a garment, so will the perpetual flame consume them. This is also written at the end of this prophecy: Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be quenched.

The master of the church has many names: being called the Father, the way, the life, the light, the arm, the propitiation, the foundation, the door, the sinless one, the treasure, Lord, God, Son, the only begotten, the form of God, the image of God. So it is with the church itself. Does one name suffice to present the whole truth? By no means. But for this reason there are countless names, that we may learn something concerning God, though it is but a small part.

O Lord, have mercy on us: for we have waited for you: be their arm in the morning, and our salvation in the time of tribulation. At the voice of the Angel the peoples fled, at your exaltation the nations were scattered. And your spoils will be gathered as the young locust is collected, as when the ditches are full of it. The Lord is magnified, for he has dwelt on high: he has filled Zion with judgment and righteousness. And there will be faith in your times: the riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge: the fear of the Lord is itself his treasure. LXX: O Lord, have mercy on us, for we trust in you: the seed of the unbelieving has come to perdition, but our salvation is in the time of tribulation: because of the voice of fear the peoples were astonished at the fear of you, and the nations were scattered. But now your spoils will be gathered, small and great: as if someone were gathering locusts, so will they mock you: holy is God who dwells on high. Zion is filled with judgment and righteousness; they will be handed over in the law; in treasures is our salvation: wisdom has come, and discipline, and piety from the Lord; these are the treasures of righteousness. The Hebrews think that the preceding section, in which we read: Woe to you who plunder: will you not yourself be plundered? and the rest to the end, was spoken against Sennacherib king of the Assyrians: that after he had overthrown the cities of the ten tribes, which were called Israel, and had also taken the cities of Judea, except Jerusalem, he himself would be overcome, and his army would be destroyed when the Angel struck. Hence they contend that the things contained in the present section are now spoken in the person of the people giving thanks to God and saying: O Lord, have mercy on us, we have waited for you: that he himself was the arm and the strength of the people hemmed in by the siege, in the morning time, and their salvation in need and distress. For at the voice of the Angel, which Symmachus rendered just as it is written in the Hebrew, AMUN (המון), and whom the Hebrews hold to be Gabriel and to have the etymology of people, the Assyrian fled, and at the exaltation of God the nations that were with him were scattered this way and that. As they fled, the spoils were gathered by the Jews, as a multitude of young locusts and of locusts is usually gathered when they have been heaped up in ditches. In their victory the Lord was magnified, and Zion was filled with judgment and righteousness, and the faith of the besieged people was proven; and they had all their riches in wisdom, and in the knowledge of God and the fear of the Lord, who alone was their treasure. These things they may say according to the history, striving by every means to overthrow the mysteries of Christ and of his Apostles. But we, after the blessedness of the Apostles, of whom it was said above (cf. Isa 32:20): Blessed are those who sow upon every water, where the ox and the ass tread, and after the lamentation and wailing of those who persecuted them, of whom it is said in what follows: Woe to those who make you wretched; but no one makes you wretched: and as a moth in a garment, so will they be worn away, prove that these things are spoken in the person of the same Apostles and of all believers. And the sense is: Lord, we have hoped in your help, and we trust in you: the seed of the unbelieving has perished for ever, and our salvation has appeared in the time of tribulation. For when you gave help, the whole multitude of the nations was scattered, and became a prey and a mockery to the victors. And this came about because the holy Lord dwells on high, and Zion is filled with judgment and righteousness, of which it was written above: Judgment and righteousness will rest in the desert. This, then, is Zion, which before was called the desert; and whoever dwells in her, to him will be handed over the law of the Gospel, in whose treasure is our salvation, and the wisdom of believers, and discipline and piety, or faith, which properly belongs to Christians, and the fear of the Lord, in which the treasures of wisdom are contained.

717. Second, in the person of the people, he asks for confirmation of the threat from God: O Lord, have mercy on us: glorify your hand and extend your arm (Sir 36:7); give us, O Lord, help from trouble (Ps 59:13[60:11]).

718. Third, he sets out the fulfillment of this petition, first, setting out the destruction of the Assyrians as to the dispersion of their army: at the voice of the angel, killing many, the people, the Assyrians who were left remaining, above: and his princes fleeing shall be afraid (Isa 31:9).

As to the plundering of their spoils: and, you, O Assyrians, your spoils shall be gathered together, by the Jews, above: they shall rejoice before you, as they that rejoice in taking a prey, when they divide the spoils (Isa 9:3).

Second, the fruit of the destruction, namely, the glory of God: the Lord is magnified: your mercy is magnified even to the heavens: and your truth unto the clouds (Ps 56:11[57:10]); and the grace of men in rectitude of action, he, namely, the Lord, has filled Zion with judgment, which is the execution of justice.

Whoever then has been established in this perfect love is sure to mount by a higher stage to that still more sublime fear belonging to love, which is the outcome of no dread of punishment or greed of reward, but of the greatest love; whereby a son fears with earnest affection a most indulgent father, or a brother fears his brother, a friend his friend, or a wife her husband, while there is no dread of his blows or reproaches, but only of a slight injury to his love, and while in every word as well as act there is ever care taken by anxious affection lest the warmth of his love should cool in the very slightest degree towards the object of it. And one of the prophets has finely described the grandeur of this fear, saying: "Wisdom and knowledge are the riches of salvation: the fear of the Lord is his treasure." He could not describe with greater clearness the worth and value of that fear than by saying that the riches of our salvation, which consist in true wisdom and knowledge of God, can only be preserved by the fear of the Lord. To this fear then not sinners but saints are invited by the prophetic word where the Psalmist says: "O fear the Lord, all ye His Saints: for they that fear Him lack nothing." For where a man fears the Lord with this fear it is certain that nothing is lacking to his perfection. For it was clearly of that other penal fear that the Apostle John said that "He who feareth is not made perfect in love, for fear hath punishment." There is then a great difference between this fear, to which nothing is lacking, which is the treasure of wisdom and knowledge, and that imperfect fear which is called "the beginning of wisdom," and which has in it punishment and so is expelled from the hearts of those who are perfect by the incoming of the fulness of love. For "there is no fear in love, but perfect love casteth out fear." And in truth if the beginning of wisdom consists in fear, what will its perfection be except in the love Of Christ which, as it contains in it the fear which belongs to perfect love, is called not the beginning but the treasure of wisdom and knowledge?
The First Conference of Abbot Chaeremon, Chapter 13

But, since there are many kinds of treasures and different grounds for joy, each one's treasure corresponds to the movement of their desire. If it is an appetite for earthly things, it makes those who share in it not happy but wretched. Those who "savor the things above, not what is on earth," and are not eager for what perishes but for what is eternal, have hidden, incorruptible resources, in that about which the prophet says, "In your treasure is our salvation. There wisdom and knowledge and holiness are from the Lord. These are the treasures of his justice."Through them, with God's grace helping us, even earthly goods are transformed into heavenly, as long as many use their wealth, either left them by law or otherwise acquired, as instruments of goodness. When they distribute, from what they can count as overabundance, to the support of the poor, they collect for themselves riches that cannot be lost, so that what they have withdrawn for alms cannot be credited to expense, and they properly keep their heart where they have "their treasure." It is most blessed to use wealth of this kind that it may grow, and not fear lest it be destroyed.

But "true wealth" signifies either the joy of eternal life itself, concerning which it is written, "the riches of his inheritance in the saints," or those spiritual virtues with which the fullness of life is attained, about which Isaiah said, "the riches of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge; the fear of the Lord himself is its treasure.""And if you are unfaithful with goods that are not yours, who will give you something of your own?" The resources of this world are alien to us, that is, external to the nature of our habitat, "for we brought nothing into this world and we are without doubt unable to take anything from it." Our possession is the kingdom of heaven, our life is Christ, and our wealth consists in the fruitfulness of spiritual works, about which Solomon said, "The redemption of a man's soul is his wealth."

Behold, those who see will cry outside: the Angels of peace will weep bitterly. The ways are laid waste, the one who passed along the path has ceased, the covenant has been made void, he has cast off the cities, he has not regarded men. The earth has mourned and languished, Lebanon is confounded and has become deaf, and Sharon has become like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel are shaken. Now I will rise up, says the Lord: now I will be exalted, now I will be lifted up. You will conceive burning heat, you will bring forth stubble; your spirit, like fire, will devour you. And the peoples will be like ashes from a burning: thorns gathered together will be burned with fire. The Hebrew word ARELLAM (אראלם), for which Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translated I will appear to them, dividing the last syllable and reading ARE LAHEM (ארא להם), the Hebrews think signifies Angels, and that this is a prophecy, after the calling of the nations and the riches of the Church, of the overthrow of the Temple: that the Angels will weep, no longer dwelling within, but going outside; and those who before were messengers of peace will weep bitterly. Or the Apostles themselves, who had been sent to announce peace to Jerusalem, to which the Lord said: If you too had known the things that belong to your peace (Luke 19:42), and to whom the Lord appeared, to strengthen them by his sight, will weep for Jerusalem, because it did not receive their preaching, because the ways are laid waste, and the one who passed along the righteous path has ceased, according to what is said in the Lamentations of Jeremiah: The ways of Zion mourn, because there are none who come to the solemnity (Lam 1:4). The covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob has also been made void: He has cast off the cities of Judea: he has not regarded men, who by their own fault chose to be beasts.

But if you want to see that the ancient prophets were terribly sad and aggrieved about the future blinding of their nation, which was the cause of our illumination, listen to Isaiah, for when he was sent to announce beforehand the grace of the Lord's coming, saying that "a light has arisen upon those who dwell in the region of the shadow of death," he responded immediately to the advent of the same light, saying "you have enlarged the nation; you have not increased its joy." And elsewhere, while commemorating the despondency of this people, Isaiah said, among other things, "the messengers of peace will weep bitterly, referring to the prophetic heralds of the divine word."

720. Behold they that see shall cry. Here he sets out the punishment which Assyria inflicted on others.

And first, he describes the punishment inflicted by them as to the disturbance of men: they that see the magnitude of the army shall cry without, they who live in the suburbs, angels of peace, envoys of Ezechias to Rabsaces, below (Isa 36:3). Behold the voice of the daughter of my people from a far country (Jer 8:19).

As to the loneliness of the ways: the ways are made desolate: the ways of Zion mourn, because there are none that come to the solemn feast (Lam 1:4); as to the breaking of covenants: the covenant is made void, namely, the covenant by which Sennacherib had insured Ezechias, and therefore, he has rejected, as if despising their friendship, he has not regarded, because of the pride of his heart: he swallows the ground, neither doth he regard when the noise of the trumpet sounds (Job 39:24).

The earth has mourned and languished for those who dwelt in the land (Gen 15 and 22). Lebanon is confounded and has become deaf: without doubt it signifies the Temple, of which we read in Zechariah: Open your gates, O Lebanon, that fire may devour your cedars (Zech 11:1). Or Jerusalem, which in Ezekiel is called Lebanon, when the Prophet says: A great eagle with great wings, which has the design of entering into Lebanon (Ezek 17:3); which the divine word afterward interprets: when, it says, Nebuchadnezzar came to Jerusalem; plainly explaining the Eagle as the king of Babylon, and Lebanon as Jerusalem. Sharon has become like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel are shaken. For Bashan, the LXX translated Galilee, the province in place of one place of the province. Sharon, moreover, is the name of the whole region around Joppa and Lydda, in which very broad and fertile plains stretch out. Bashan too is a region beyond the Jordan, which the two and a half tribes possessed, and which means most fruitful and fat (Deut 3); and Carmel, of which we spoke above. The once fertile places of Judea, then, will be turned into a wilderness, by which it is shown μεταφορικῶς that all the opulence of the Jews is to be exchanged for want and poverty. Since, then, they would not receive the word of the Apostles, Lebanon is confounded, and Sharon is turned into a wilderness, and Bashan and Carmel are shaken.
As to the destruction of regions: the land has mourned, and languished, and he names especially fertile regions; above (Isa 24:4, 7) has the same thing.
Therefore the Lord says that he will rise up, either from his very great patience, or from the underworld, and will be exalted among the nations, and lifted up on the cross.

721. Second, he sets out divine resistance to his efforts: now will I rise up. And concerning this, he sets out three things.

On the part of God, the intention of resisting: now, namely, after he has done such evils, will I rise up, against him: by reason of the misery of the needy, and the groans of the poor, now will I arise, says the Lord (Ps 11:6[12:5]).

And he turns in apostrophe to the Jews themselves: You will conceive burning heat, and you will bring forth stubble, and your spirit will kindle a fire for you, so that the devouring flame may consume what was conceived and brought forth.

And the peoples of the Jews, he says, will be like ashes from a burning, showing the greatness of their misfortune by the remnants of the embers. For their thorns, which have been gathered together by the multitude of their sins, will be devoured by the burning; which most refer to the last captivity and overthrow of Jerusalem. Others affirm that it will come about more fully and perfectly at the time of judgment.

Third, he sets out the manner of the resistance or of the punishment: and the people shall be as ashes after a fire, because their bodies were literally reduced to ashes; thorns, that is, the Assyrians, because they were tearing others: you shall tread down the wicked when they shall be ashes under the sole of your feet (Mal 4:3).

He speaks moreover concerning our ears, how He hath circumcised both them and our heart. The Lord saith in the prophet, "In the hearing of the ear they obeyed me." And again He saith, "By hearing, those shall hear who are afar off; they shall know what I have done." And, "Be ye circumcised in your hearts, saith the Lord." ... Therefore He hath circumcised our ears, that we might hear His word and believe.
The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter IX

Hear, you who are far off, what I have done, and you who are near, know my strength. The sinners in Zion are terrified, trembling has seized the hypocrites. Who of you can dwell with devouring fire? Who of you will dwell with everlasting burnings? He who walks in acts of righteousness, and speaks truths, who casts away avarice from calumny, and shakes his hands free of every bribe, who stops his ears lest he hear blood, and shuts his eyes lest he see evil. He will dwell on high; fortresses of rocks are his height: bread has been given him, his waters are faithful. His eyes will see the king in his beauty: they will behold the land from afar. Your heart will meditate fear. Where is the scribe? Where is he who weighs the words of the law? Where is the teacher of little ones? You will not see the imprudent people, the people of deep speech, so that you cannot understand the eloquence of its tongue, in which there is no wisdom. LXX: Those who are far off will hear what they have done: those who draw near will know my strength. The lawless who were in Zion have departed; trembling will seize the impious. Who will announce to you that fire is burning? Who will announce to you the eternal place? He who walks in righteousness, and speaks the right way, and hates impiety and iniquity, and shakes his hands free of gifts, and stops his ears so as not to hear the judgment of blood, and shuts his eyes so that they may not see iniquity, he will dwell in a lofty cave of a very strong rock. Bread will be given him, and his water will be faithful: your eyes will see the king with glory, they will see the land from afar; your soul will meditate fear. Where are the grammarians? Where are the counselors? Where is he who numbers those who nourish both the small and the great people? To whom he did not give counsel: nor did he know his deep voice, so that the despised people did not hear, and there is no understanding for the one who hears. Since the ways are laid waste, the one who passed along the paths has ceased, the covenant with the people of the Jews has been made void, God has cast off their cities and has not counted them among men; therefore you who are far off, hear what I have done, and draw near, that you may know my strength.

The Scripture itself … expressly distinguishes between Abraham's bosom, where the poor man dwells, and the infernal place of torment. "Hell" (I take it) means one thing, and "Abraham's bosom" another. "A great gulf" is said to separate those regions and to hinder a passage from one to the other. Besides, the rich man could not have "lifted up his eyes," and from a distance too, except to a superior height, and from the said distance all up through the vast immensity of height and depth.… There is some determinate place called Abraham's bosom, and it is designed for the reception of souls of Abraham's children, even from among the Gentiles (since he is "the father of many nations," which must be classed amongst his family), and of the same faith as that with which he himself believed God, without the yoke of the law and the sign of circumcision. This region, therefore, I call Abraham's bosom. Although it is not in heaven, it is yet higher than hell, and it is appointed to afford an interval of rest to the souls of the righteous, until the consummation of all things shall complete the resurrections of all people with the "full recompense of their reward." This consummation will then be manifested in heavenly promises.… Amos, however, tells us of "those stories towards heaven" which Christ "builds"—of course for his people. There also is that everlasting abode of which Isaiah asks, "Who shall declare to you the eternal place, but he (that is, of course, Christ) who walks in righteousness, speaks of the straight path, and hates injustice and iniquity?" Now, although this everlasting abode is promised, and the ascending stories (or steps) to heaven are built by the Creator, who further promises that the seed of Abraham shall be even as the stars of heaven, by virtue certainly of the heavenly promise, why may it not be possible, without any injury to that promise, that by Abraham's bosom is meant some temporary receptacle of faithful souls, wherein is even now delineated an image of the future and where is given some foresight of the glory of both judgments?

The sinners, or the impious, who were in Zion are terrified, or have departed, and trembling has seized the hypocrites, to whom the Lord said in the Gospel: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites (Matt 23:14)! Who of you can dwell with him who is a devouring fire? Who will dwell with everlasting burnings? Or according to the LXX: Who will announce to you that the eternal fire is burning, which God has prepared for the devil and his angels?

"He looked upon them, and the nations shook and the mountains quickly scattered." The sight of the Lord shattered what was hardened and melted what was tightly compact, so that the truth expressed by Isaiah might be evident, for God is a living fire who advances to purify, not to kill: "Who among you can dwell with the devouring fire, or who among you can walk with eternal flames?" Whomever he looks upon, therefore, and touches with his warmth, he melts on the spot. Consequently, when he will later look upon the nations with mercy and judge them to be most worthy of redemption through his Christ, immediately their hardness will be shattered.
COMMENTARY ON THE CANTICLE OF HABAKKUK 6:5

Second, he shows the sign of his power, the sinners, namely, the Assyrians, are broken: I will break this people, and this city, as the potter's vessel is broken (Jer 19:11).

723. Which of you can. Here he invites to consider the fitness of him that lives with God, that he may be always inviolate, protected by him.

And first, he examines the fit,

second, he excludes the unworthy: where is the learned (Isa 33:18).

Concerning the first, he does three things.

First, he sets out the question: which of you can dwell with devouring fire, namely, with God, that he not be devoured by him, like the Assyrians: the Lord your God is a consuming fire (Deut 4:24).

Who, then, will be able to dwell with God, or to announce the punishments to come? Everyone who is such as the prophetic word describes: who walks in many acts of righteousness, and loves acts of righteousness not once but always, and speaks truths not on one occasion but continually; who casts away avarice, which is the mother of calumny. For money is not heaped up for one man except with another's loss and harm. And he shakes his hands free of every bribe; for bribes blind the eyes even of the wise. He stops his ears lest he hear the judgment of blood. All iniquity and oppression and injustice is a judgment of blood: and though one does not kill with the sword, yet he slays by his will. And he shuts his eyes lest he see evil. Happy the conscience that neither hears nor beholds evil.

There are some who indeed do not receive rewards of money from ordination, yet bestow sacred orders for human favor, and from that very generosity seek only the recompense of praise. These certainly do not bestow freely what was freely received, because from the service of holiness they have rendered, they seek the coin of favor. Hence the prophet spoke well when describing the just man, saying: Who shakes his hands free from every gift. For he does not say: Who shakes his hands from a gift, but added from every, because one thing is a gift from service, another a gift from the hand, another a gift from the tongue. A gift from service is deference unduly rendered, a gift from the hand is money, a gift from the tongue is favor. Therefore he who bestows sacred orders shakes his hands free from every gift when in divine matters he seeks not only no money, but also no human favor.
40 Homilies on the Gospels, Homily IV

We must bear in mind too that there are three ways in which deceit itself is practised, in that, surely, the object aimed at in it is either the secret interest of our fellow creatures' feelings, or the breath of applause, or some outward advantage; contrary to which it is rightly said of the righteous man by the prophet, "Blessed is he that shaketh his hands clear of every favour." For as deceit does not consist only in the receiving of money; so, no doubt, a favour is not confined to one thing, but there are three ways of receiving favours after which deceit goeth in haste. For a favour from the heart, is interest solicited in the opinion, a favour from the mouth is glory from applause, a favour from the head a reward by gift. Now every righteous man 'shaketh his hands clear of every favour,' in that in whatever he does aright, he neither aims to win vainglory from the affections of his fellow creatures, nor applause from their lips, nor a gift from their hands. And so he alone is not guilty of deceit in doing God's work, who while he is energetic in studying right conduct, neither pants after the rewards of earthly substance, nor after words of applause, nor after favour in man's judgment. Therefore because our very good actions themselves cannot escape the sword of ambushed sin, unless they be guarded every day by anxious fear, it is rightly said in this place by the holy man, I was afraid of all my works.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 9
Taking bribes is a violation of the truth. Therefore, it is said of the just man: "He who cleanses his hands of every gift will live on the heights."

724. Second, he shows fitness, removing three things to which the Jews were prone, namely, avarice as to things taken away unjustly: that casts away avarice by oppression, and as to things received illiberally, and shakes his hands from all bribes; second, as to cruelty in homicide: that stops his ears lest he hear blood; third, as to lust: and shuts his eyes that he may see no evil.

He, then, who is such will dwell on high, that is, in the kingdom of heaven, or in a lofty cave of a very strong rock, in Christ Jesus: the rock that followed the people of Israel, that they might drink from it and be protected by its strength. Bread will be given him, and his waters are faithful: which the fables of the Gentiles understand as ambrosia and nectar. But we shall interpret the bread and the most faithful waters as the law of God.

By the name of bread the teaching of perfection is shown, as Paul attests, who, rousing the weak to conversion, says: "I gave you milk to drink, not solid food. For you were not yet able, nor are you yet able." For if milk belongs to little ones, bread belongs to none but the perfect. Whence also it is said of the strength of the perfect man: "He shall dwell on high, the fortifications of rocks shall be his loftiness, bread has been given to him." Therefore in the house of bread a king is sought for anointing, because those are profitably advanced who are nourished in the order of perfect conduct. For he is able to make others strong who has not been nourished in lax and negligent conduct.

Two advents of our Lord and Savior are indicated in the Scriptures. The one [is] his first advent in the flesh, which took place without honor by reason of his being set at nothing, as Isaiah spoke of him in the past, saying, "We saw him, and he had no form nor comeliness, but his form was despised (and) rejected above all men; a man smitten and familiar with bearing infirmity (for his face was turned away); he was despised, and esteemed not." But his second advent is announced as glorious, when he shall come from heaven with the host of angels and the glory of his Father, as the prophet says, "You shall see the King in glory"; and, "I saw one like the Son of man coming with the clouds of heaven; and he came to the Ancient of Days, and he was brought to him. And there were given him dominion, and honor, and glory, and the kingdom; all tribes and languages shall serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away."

He, then, who is such will behold Christ the king in his brightness, of whom it is said above (cf. Isa 32:1): Behold, a righteous king will reign, and princes will rule in judgment. And his eyes will see from afar the land which they had long desired, the land of the meek and gentle, of which it is written in the Gospel: Blessed are the meek, for they will possess the land (Matt 5:4); or, set in heaven, they will look down on earthly things.

But it also must be noted that the Savior's tomb, above which a memorial canopy is often seen, can properly be called a cave or a den. Clearly, then, it was about the Lord Jesus Christ in the tomb that the prophet prophesied, "He lived in a high cave of fortified rocks," and shortly thereafter added, with regard to the apostles rejoicing at the resurrection of the Lord: "You will see the king in his glory."

Through the sacraments of his humanity with which we have been imbued, we may be able to attain the contemplation of the glory of his divinity, that contemplation which he himself in his faithful benevolence pledged to his faithful servants when he said, "One who has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. One who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him." He says, "I will manifest myself"—that is, "Not in such a way that everyone can look at me, or in such a way that even the unfaithful can see me and crucify me, but in such a way that only the pure eyes of the saints can see 'the King of ages in his beauty.' " In this way I will show myself to those who love me, so as to reward them for their love. Therefore let us hope, as we have said, that through the visible nature of his humanity we may be able to ascend to see the beauty of his divinity, if we keep these sacraments as we have received them, unblemished in the worthy honor of justice and holiness and truth, if we follow his example in his human way of life, and if we humbly follow the words of the teaching which he ministered to us through his humanity.

The disciples indeed saw him coming in his kingdom, for on the mountain they saw him shining in that brightness with which he will be seen in his kingdom by all the saints when the judgment has been brought to completion. But since the eyes of the disciples were still mortal and corruptible, they were then unable to sustain what the whole church of the saints will have the power to look upon when she has become incorruptible through resurrection. Concerning this it is written, "Their eye will see the king in his beauty."

Third, as to the vision of God: his eyes shall see the king, that is, God: go forth, you daughters of Zion, and see the king Solomon (Song 3:11).

Fourth, as to holy affection, namely, contempt for earthly things: they shall see the land far off, as if far off beneath them, namely, in dignity. And these things can be explained either as to those who live with God in the present Church or also in the Church triumphant. Or otherwise: the land, namely, of the living: I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living (Ps 26[27]:13); far off, as if far above the dignity of nature or the fitness of many, now in hope, in the future in reality; and thus, this belongs with the third.

And if you want all these thoughts to diminish in you and not to have power over you, then recite in your heart without ceasing every fruit that is written in the Scriptures, having in yourself the resolution to walk in them, as it is written in Isaiah, "Your heart shall meditate on the fear"of the Lord, and all these things shall cease from you, little by little.

Your heart will meditate fear: so that when you have attained all things, you may say with the Apostle: I who am not worthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God (1 Cor 15:9). For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. Where is the scribe? Where is he who weighs the words of the law? Where is the teacher of little ones? (Prov 9:1). Where, he says, are the scribes and Pharisees, who, weighing the words of the Law in the balance, deceived the unhappy people? whom the Scripture now calls little ones: little in sense, little in understanding.

And as to divine subjection: your heart shall meditate filial fear: the fear of the Lord shall delight the heart (Sir 1:12).

728. Where is the learned? Here he excludes the unworthy as to those who seem especially worthy.

And first, the eminent in wisdom: where is the learned, educated in philosophy; where is he that pondered the words of the law, educated in divine knowledge; the teacher, instructing others in the elements of either: where is the wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the learned? (1 Cor 1:20).

And when the eyes of the believer have beheld the king in his majesty, and his heart has meditated fear, then he will not see the imprudent people, the people of the Jews, or of the philosophers and orators of the world, who applaud themselves for secular learning and eloquence, of whom he now says: A people of deep speech, so that you cannot understand the eloquence of its tongue; whose whole adornment is in words, who have only the leaves and the shade of speech, and do not possess the fruit of truth. Then there follows: In which there is no wisdom; of whom it is also said in another place: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the prudent I will reject (1 Cor 1:19). Why? Because God has made foolish the wisdom of this world.
Second, those who are eminent in eloquence, but not in wisdom: the people of profound speech: behold I will bring upon you a nation whose language you shall not know (Jer 5:15).

Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnity: your eyes will see Jerusalem, a wealthy habitation: a tabernacle that can by no means be moved, nor will its pegs be taken away for ever, and none of its cords will be broken. For only there is our Lord magnificent: a place of rivers, streams very broad and open; no ship with oars will pass through it, nor will a great trireme cross it. For the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king; he himself will save us. Your cords are loosened, and will not hold: so will your mast be, that you cannot spread out the ensign. Then the spoils of many preys will be divided: the lame will seize the plunder. Nor will the neighbor say, I am faint: the people that dwells in it, iniquity will be taken away from it. LXX: Behold Zion, the city, our salvation: your eyes will see Jerusalem, a rich city, tabernacles that will not be moved: nor will the stakes of its tabernacle be taken away for ever, and its cords will not be torn apart: for the name of the Lord is great to you: your place will be rivers and streams very broad and spacious: no ship driven by oars will go in through it: for my God is great: the Lord will not pass me by, our judge, the Lord our prince, the Lord our king, the Lord himself will save us. Your cords are broken because they did not hold: your mast is bent, so that it lets the sails go: it will not raise the ensign until it is given over to devastation. Many lame, therefore, will take spoils: and they will not say, I shall labor; the people that dwells in them, their sin will be forgiven them. O righteous one, to whom it was said above: your heart will meditate fear; and, the imprudent people you will not see; and who had heard before, your eyes will see the king in his beauty: look upon Zion, the city of our solemnity, see the Church of Christ, in which is the true solemnity: your eyes will behold the vision of peace, and riches beyond hope, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man, and the tabernacle that can by no means be moved. For the former tabernacle, which the people of the Jews had, was moved and taken away. Nor will its pegs be moved for ever, and all its cords will be firm; so that the Lord dwells in it, which is the place of all the rivers and running streams, through which no one of the opposing side will be able to sail: nor a great trireme, which is interpreted as the devil, will be able to cross it: because the Lord himself is our judge, and prince, and king, and Savior, and under his protection we shall fear the snares of no one. These things are said of Zion, the city of our solemnity, and of Jerusalem, the richest habitation, which the Lord himself will surround and fortify with his rivers.

729. Look upon Zion. Here he leads to consideration of the worthiness of the liberated city.

And first, as to its abundance of goods, setting out four things which are in the heavenly or the militant Church, namely,

joy of heart: the city of our solemnity, above: as in the voice of the sanctified solemnity, and joy of heart (Isa 30:29).

Wealth of goods: your eyes shall see Jerusalem, a rich habitation, above: and my people shall sit in the beauty of peace, and in the tabernacles of confidence, and in wealthy rest (Isa 32:18).

The grace of immovability: a tabernacle that cannot be removed; nails: this is said according to the likeness of a tabernacle fastened with nails and cords, which are loosed when it must be moved: his power is an everlasting power that shall not be taken away: and his kingdom that shall not be destroyed (Dan 7:14). And he assigns the reason for this: because only the Lord, who has the power to move it, and others cannot: great is the Lord, and exceedingly to be praised (Ps 47:2[48:1]).

For the plainly spoken words of these interpreting have made the sentences of the ancient Fathers henceforth clear to us. Hence the Prophet Isaiah viewing the words plain by the interpretation of Holy Church, not obscured by the darkness of allegories, exclaimed, saying, "The place of rivers, the broadest and open streams." For the sayings of the Old Testament were as narrow and close streams, which bound up the sentences of their lore in the darkest gathering together. But on the other hand the teaching of Holy Church are 'streams both broad and open,' because her declarations are at once many in number to those that find them, and plain to those that seek.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 18

Abundance of waters: a place of rivers, that is, of divine admonitions; streams, diverse modes of participation: the stream of the river makes the city of God joyful (Ps 45:5).

Nonetheless, the Jews fabulously refer all this to the golden age of Jerusalem.

730. Second, as to its freedom from evils: no ship with oars, belonging to any of their enemies, who were accustomed to harass the promised land by way of the sea, has passed by it, using the past tense for the future; the great galley (trieris), a ship having three rows of oars.
And he assigns the cause: for the Lord is our judge, judging us by our adversaries: behold your king comes to you, meek (Zech 9:9).

But now he speaks to the earthly Jerusalem: that the cords of its tabernacle are loosened, and could not hold up the tent, and its mast, on which the most beautiful sails once hung, has fallen with its ropes broken, so that it is useless not only for sailing but also for an ensign. And after their ship has been broken up and the tabernacle scattered, so that the cords are torn apart on both sides, the plunder will be divided among the victors: who will be so weak in their own strength that they are called lame; and nonetheless, since the wrath of God gives them strength, they will feel no weakness, nor will they say: I have labored. For whoever is among them, iniquity and sin will be taken away from him, because he has carried out the will of God.

731. Your tacklings are loosed. Here he foretells the destruction of the ungrateful Jews, carried out afterwards by the Romans, and he sets out three things.

First, their powerlessness to resist: your tacklings are loosed, that is, prepared, that you may defend yourself against the Romans. This is said according to a likeness of a ship which is prepared for the same. Your mast (malus), the mast (arbor) of the ship, that is, the temple, in which the precious vessels and veils are known to have been: the Lord has delivered me into a hand, out of which I am not able to flee (Lam 1:14).
